english: Not because 'righteousness has persecuted me' [Ps 22:19], but do not forsake me, do not become distant from me. God forsakes someone when they are worthy to suffer grievous things. I do not say this to mean that He tests them with grievous things; He is not not-forsaking, but when one, having grievous things, is defeated and cast down, then You do not forsake me, if You do not depart from me. I have clung to You; I have become one spirit toward You. When one clings to the Lord, and the Lord to him. 'My soul has clung to You behind You' [Ps 63:8].

Cry out for my help, O Lord of my salvation [Ps 27:7]. You stand away from me if I sin, not if I am hated unjustly, nor even if some magnify themselves against me. And You are Lord and God of my salvation. But salvation does not touch the flesh, nor is it found regarding external things, but regarding the soul itself. This is the said eternal salvation; for it 'became'—the Christ, clearly—'eternal salvation to all those obeying Him.' The flesh's 'eternal salvation', which doctors bring to it, or that which a pilot saves for those sailing, is not eternal; for these will soon die again. But the salvation of God is eternal; He is their salvation.

1–2 To the end, to Ithium. I said: I will guard my ways so as not to sin in my tongue. This is one of the Psalms. In Ezra and in the [Book of the] Remaining, there is a memory of each name of those being submitted. And this, then, is one of them, or perhaps he himself composed the psalm for David, or having received it from David, he proclaimed it. And it is the work of the Psalms to say their psalms, both those they themselves composed and those others arranged.

This, then, is a victory song. Often the sinner is troubled by these things, but after conquering and trampling him and taking him under hand, [the psalmist] sends back the song; for no one sings a victory song while still warring and being warred against, but in the having conquered. Likewise, Moses and all the Jewish multitude did not say a victory song when they were against Pharaoh, but when they saw him become a drowning man: 'Let us sing to the Lord, for gloriously He has been glorified; He has cast horse and rider into the sea' [Ex 15:1]. When the horse and its rider were cast into the sea, and Pharaoh's chariots and the power of the...

God cast the Red Sea into the sea, and then a victorious song was appropriately sent up. And David says in the seventy-first psalm: 'In the day when he rescued him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, then he said: I will love you, O Lord my strength' (Ps 71:5), and all the rest which the song contains. It is a prayer before the war and in the war, but a victorious hymn and song after the destruction of the war, after capturing the enemies.

I said: 'I will guard my ways so as not to sin in my tongue' (Ps 34:13). For almost every practical sin has its beginning in the word. Regarding the young man whom the prostitute—who is personified in the proverbs, that is, being a woman or a false glory or a deception starting from words—is able to ensnare: for it is said, 'She led him astray with much intercourse' or enticement, and 'with the nooses through the lips she hollowed him out' (Prov 2:3/7). And behold, the word has become the beginning of sin. And the elders, indeed, those remaining according to Sophronius, started a word toward her.

If, therefore, someone does not sin in the tongue, he guards the ways well; for he said that the beginning of these ways is the word. And from the opposite of all good works, the word is the beginning. But he does not speak only about those ways; he added, 'so as not to sin in my tongue' (Ps 34:13). Yet sinning in the tongue is not the same as saying, 'My tongue will meditate on your righteousness' (Ps 119:9). 'The beginning of your words is truth' (Ps 119:160). The cause of saying your words is your truth; I will make this manifest if I know it. Therefore, upon the virtues and the well-flowing ways, truth is the beginning, the cause. But upon the forbidden ways, from which it is necessary to guard oneself and from which it is proper to turn away, the word is the beginning, as has already been said.

I set a guard upon my mouth (Ps 34:13). Remember how he said 'not to sin in the tongue': 'I set a guard upon my mouth.' Since 'from the words someone is justified and from his words he is condemned' (Matt 12:37), it is necessary for the mouth to place a guard, so that I may say the [good] things and not the [bad], that we may speak the profitable things and be silent about the harmful ones; for no one is able at once to bring forth words that both justify and condemn. Something like this is said with an enigma in the proverbs: 'Death and life are in the hand of the tongue' (Prov 18:21). And the 'hand' of the 'tongue' is the word.

source_text: ἐνέργεια γλώσσης. ὁ λαλῶν τὰ ὠφε̣λοῦντα καὶ εἰς βασιλείαν εἰσάγοντα ζωὴν ἔχει ἐν τῇ γλώσσῃ. ὁ δὲ τὰ ἐναντία καὶ ἀπηγορευμένα, θάν̣ατο̣ν ἔχει ἐν τῷ λόγῳ ἑαυτοῦ "γλῶσσαν" ὀνομαζομένῳ. καὶ ἐν ἄλλῃ γραφῇ λέγει ὅτι· "τοῖς λόγοις σου ποίησον ζυγὸν καὶ σταθμόν". ἐσταθμισμένως δεῖ λέγειν, ζυγὸν δεῖ ἔχειν καὶ βάλλειν ἐφ' ἑκάστης τρυτάνης τοὺς λόγους̣. καὶ ἐὰν καταταλαντεύωσιν οἱ ὀρθοὶ λόγοι, ἐκείνους αἱρεῖσθαι καὶ ἀπαγγέλλειν προσήκει, τοὺς δὲ φαύλους ἀποστρέφεσθαι. πάλιν λέγεται· "χείλη σοφῶν δέδεται αἰσθήσει". ὅταν ᾐσθημένως λέγῃ τις, δέδεται τὰ χείλη, οὐ παντὶ λόγῳ αὐτὰ ἀνοίγει, ἀλλὰ τῷ ὠφελ̣οῦν̣τι. "τὰ χείλη μου ἀνοίξω καὶ τὸ στόμα μου ἀναγγελεῖ τὴν αἴ νεσίν σου". ὁ δεδεμένα τὰ χείλη ἔχων αἰσθήσει αἰσ̣θηθεὶς ὅτι ὠφελοῦντά ἐστιν ἃ με´̣λ̣λει λέγειν, ἤνοιξεν αὐτά. 273 ὅταν δὲ βλάπτωσιν τὰ προφερόμενα, κλείει καὶ δεσμεῖ τὰ χείλη τῇ αἰσθήσει, δεσμεῖ τὸν λόγον. 2–3 ἐν τῷ συνστῆναι τὸν ἁμαρτωλὸν ἐναντίον μου ἐκωφώθην καὶ ἐταπεινώθην καὶ ἐσίγησα ἐξ ἀγαθῶν. πολλάκις ἐπιφαινόμενος ὁ ἁμαρτωλὸς ἐρεθίζει καὶ ἐκκαλεῖται εἰς τὰ φίλα αὐτῷ. ἄν ποτε οὖν συνστῇ, παρ' ἡμᾶς δὲ γίνεται αὐτὸν τὸ συνστῆναι· εἰ μὴ γὰρ δῶμεν αὐτῷ τόπον, οὐ δύναται συνστῆναι. τὸ συνστῆναι δὲ οὕτως συνστάδην πολεμῆσ̣αι. δεῖ σιωπῆσαι· ἐρεθίζει γὰρ πολλάκις· διὰ τοῦτο γὰρ συνστὰς ὁ ὄφις κατέναντι τῆς Εὕας ἠρέθιζεν αὐτῆς τὸν λόγον καὶ ἔβλαψεν αὐτήν. ἔδει δὲ σιωπῆσαι καὶ αἴσθησιν λαβόντα τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ἀσθενείας ἢ τῆς προλαβούσης ἁμαρτίας μὴ λαλῆσαί τι πρὸς αὐτόν, ἀλλὰ σιγῆσαι ἐξ ἀγαθῶν. τὸ δὲ "σιγᾶν ἐξ ἀγαθῶν" οὐ τοῦτο λέγει "μὴ λέγειν τὰ ἀγαθά", ἀλλ' ἐκ τῶν ἀγαθῶν σιωπὴν ἔχειν νενοημένην. οἷον ἀρετὴν ἀναλαβὼν σώφρονος ἔγνων ὅτι οὐ δεῖ α᾿̣ποκριθῆναι ἐκ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ, τουτέστιν τῆς σωφροσύνης. ἐσιώπησα πρὸς τὴν συνστάδην φανεῖσαν καὶ ἐρεθίζουσαν εἰς ἁμαρτίαν. εἰ τοίνυν ὁ νεανίας ἐκεῖνος μηδὲν ἦν ἀποκρινόμενος ἀπὸ νοήσεως ὀρθῆς πρὸς τὴν πόρνην, οὐκ "ἀπεπλανᾶτο πολλῇ ὁμιλίᾳ" οὐδὲ "ἡλίσκετο βρόχοις τῶν χειλέων ἑαυτοῦ". ἐσίγησα οὖν ἐπελθόντων μοι τῶν ἀγαθῶν τῶν πειθόντων με μὴ ἀποκρίνασθαι ἐκείνῳ. οὐ λέγ̣ε̣ι· "ε᾿̣σίγησα, ἵνα μὴ λαλῶ τὰ ἀγαθά", ἀλλ' "ἵνα μὴ λαλῶ τὰ ἐρεθίζοντα". γέγονέν μοι δὲ αὕτη ἡ σιωπὴ ἐκ νοη´̣σεως τῶν ἀγαθῶν τῶν κωλυόντων τὴν τοιαύτην ὁμιλίαν. "ἔστιν σιωπῶν εὑρισκόμενος σοφός". ὁ οὕτω σιωπῶν εὑρίςκεται σοφός. καὶ σοφόν γέ ἐστιν τὸ γνῶναι τίνι λαλῆσαι δεῖ καὶ τίνι μὴ καὶ πότε προενεγκεῖν λόγους καὶ πότε μή. "ἔστιν" οὖν "σιωπῶν εὑρισκόμενος σοφός, καὶ ἔστιν σιωπῶν, οὐ γὰρ ἔχει ἀπόκρισιν". καὶ οὗτος ἔχει ἠρέμα τινὰ φρόνησιν· γνοὺς γὰρ ὅτι οὐκ ἔχει ἀπόκρισιν, ἡσυχάζει. "καὶ ἔστιν σιωπῶν εἰδὼς καιρόν". οὗτος τέλειός ἐστιν. 3 καὶ τὸ ἄλγημά μου ἀνεκαινίσθη. τότε τὸ ἄλγημα ἀνακαινίζεται συνστάντος τοῦ ἁμαρτωλοῦ. ἐν ἀναπολήσει γέγονεν ὧν ἔπραξεν, ἐφ' οἷς ἀλγεῖν δεῖ. καὶ ὥςπερ ἀνακαινισμὸν ἔλαβεν τὸ ἄλγημα. ἐνκαινισμὸς δέ ἐστιν τὸ οἰκῆσαι ἐν οἴκῳ πρώτως. ἀνακαινισμὸς οὖν ἐστιν τὸ ἤδη μαρανθὲν καὶ ἡσυχάζον ἀγαγεῖν εἰς τὸ ἀνθεῖν. "τὸ ἄλγημά μου" οὖν "ἀνεκαινίσθη". εἰρηκὼς ὅτι· "ἐφύλαξα τὰς ὁδούς μου τοῦ μὴ ἁμαρτάνειν ἐν γλώσσῃ 184 μου", ἔγνων ὅτι ἥμαρτον. "ἀνεκαινίσθη" οὖν "τὸ ἄλγημά μου". μακάριον δέ ἐστιν τὸν ἡμαρτηκότα ἐν ἀνακαινισμῷ τοῦ ἀλγήματος γενέσθαι καὶ μὴ τῆς ἡδονῆς· ὁ γὰρ χαίρων ἐφ' οἷς ἔπραξεν καὶ αὖθις αὐτὰ εἰς μέσον φέρων ἀνακαινίζει. ὁ δὲ ἀλγῶν αἰσθηθεὶς ὅτι δεῖ φυλάττειν τὰς ὁδοὺς καὶ μὴ δεῖν ἐν γλώττῃ ἁμαρτάνειν, ἀνακαινίζειν τὸ ἄλγημα κλαίων καὶ λυπούμενος "τὴν κατὰ θεὸν λύπην τὴν μετάνοιαν ἐργαζομένην". ἐν αὐτῷ ὅλως τῷ μεταγιγνώσκειν ἀλγεῖ ὅτι ὅλως γέγονεν ἐν τοιούτοις. 4 ἐθερμάνθη ἡ καρδία μου ἐντός μου. δύναται λέγειν ὁ´̣τ̣ι· ἡ καρδία μου ὥσπερ θέρμην προσέλαβεν καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ἀνακαινισμοῦ τοῦ ἀλγήματος. δύναται δὲ καὶ τοῦτο εἰπεῖν· ἐπεὶ σφοδρῶς καθηψάμην ἐμαυτοῦ καὶ ὀλοφύρομαι καὶ ἀποκλαίομαι τὸ ἄλγημα, "ἐθερμάνθη ἡ καρδία μου", διάπυρος γέγονεν. "ἐν" αὐτῇ γοῦν "τῇ μελέτῃ μου ἐξεκάη πῦρ" ἀναλίσκον καὶ φλουρουντα με· ἦσαν γὰρ χόρτος καὶ ξύλα καὶ τὰ ἄλλα. οὐ μόνον ἐν τῷ τελειοῦσθαι ἔχω τὸ πῦρ τοῦτο τὸ ἀναλωτικὸν τῶν χορτώδων, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ μελετᾶν μου τὸ ἄλγημα. εὖ δὲ καὶ τὸ "ἐντός μου". ἐνίων ἡ καρδία θερμαίνεται ὥστε τὴν θέρμην καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ ἔξω χωρῆσαι. οἱ γοῦν̣ γαμοῦντες καὶ πυρούμενοι οὐκ ἔχουσιν ἐντὸς τὴν καρδίαν θερμανθεῖσαν, 274 ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τὰ ἔξω χωρήσασα ἔχει τὸν ἐνπρησμόν. ὥσπερ ἐὰν λέγηται· "ἐταράχθην καὶ οὐκ ἐλάλησα". ὁ
english: The activity of the tongue. He who speaks what is beneficial and leads into the kingdom of life has life in the tongue. But he who speaks the opposite and the forbidden things has death in his own word called a 'tongue'. And in another scripture it says: 'With your words make a balance and a weight' (Prov 16:11). It is necessary to speak having weighed; it is necessary to have a balance and to cast the words upon each scale. And if the upright words are found to be balanced, it is proper to choose those and to proclaim them, but to turn away from the bad ones.

Again it is said: 'The lips of the wise are taught by perception' (Ps 51:13). When someone speaks having perceived, the lips are taught, not opening them to every word, but to what is beneficial. 'I will open my lips and my mouth shall proclaim your praise' (Ps 51:14). He who has the taught lips, having perceived that what he intends to speak is beneficial, opened them. But when they harm what is being uttered, he closes and binds the lips with perception; he binds the word.

'In the standing of the sinner against me, I was made deaf and humbled, and I kept silence for the sake of good things' (Ps 31:5). Often appearing, the sinner provokes and is called out to the things pleasing to him. If, therefore, he ever stands [against us], it is our part to make him stand; for if we do not give him a place, he is not able to stand. But to stand in this way is to stand in battle. It is necessary to be silent; for he often provokes; because the serpent, having stood against Eve, provoked her word and harmed her. It was necessary to be silent, having received perception of her own weakness or of the sin that had come before, not to speak anything to her, but to keep silence for the sake of good things.

And the 'keeping silence for the sake of good things' does not say 'not to speak the good things', but to have a silence made wise from the good things. For example, having taken up virtue, a prudent man knew that he must not respond out of the good, that is, out of prudence. I kept silence toward the standing revealed and provoking toward sin. If, therefore, that young man had been responding to nothing from right understanding toward the harlot, he would not have 'been led astray by much association' (1 Tim 5:15) nor 'been enticed by the morsels of his lips' (Prov 5:3). I kept silence, therefore, when the good things had come upon me, persuading me not to respond to him. He does not say: 'I kept silence so as not to speak the good things', but 'so as not to speak the provoking things'. And this silence has become to me from...

The wisdom of the good things which hinders such a conversation. "He is found wise while being silent." He who thus remains silent is found wise. And it is indeed wisdom to know to whom one must speak and to whom one must not, and when to bring forward words and when not. "He is therefore found wise while being silent, and he is silent, for he has no answer." And this man possesses a certain quietness of mind; for having known that he has no answer, he keeps peace. "And he is wise, being silent, knowing the right time." This man is perfect.

And "my sorrow was renewed" (Psalm 39:10). Then the sorrow is renewed when the sinner stands in reflection upon what he has done, upon which it is necessary to grieve. And just as the sorrow received a renewal, renewal is to dwell in a house at first. A renewal, therefore, is to lead that which has already withered and is silent into flowering. "My sorrow" therefore "was renewed." Having said, "I kept my ways not to sin with my tongue" (Psalm 119:11), I knew that I had sinned. Therefore "my sorrow was renewed." And it is blessed for one who has sinned to experience a renewal of sorrow and not of pleasure; for he who rejoices over what he has done and brings those things back into the midst again, renews [the sin]. But he who grieves, having perceived that it is necessary to guard the ways and not to sin with the tongue, renews the sorrow, weeping and grieving, "working the sorrow according to God, which is repentance." In this, he grieves entirely in the recognizing that it has entirely happened in such matters.

"My heart was warmed within me" (Psalm 39:3). One may say: my heart has received heat just as warmth, and from the renewal of sorrow. And one may also say this: because I seized myself intensely and I am being consumed and I weep aloud the sorrow, "my heart was warmed," it has become fiery. "In" indeed "my practice, a fire burned up" (Psalm 39:2), consuming and making me ash; for they were hay and wood and other things. I have this consuming fire not only in the being perfected, but also in my practicing the sorrow. And the "within me" is also good. The heart becomes hot so that the heat spreads even to the outside. Those, indeed, who are burning with passion do not have a heart warmed within, but, having spread to the outside, they have the state of one being pressed. It is as if it were said: "I was troubled and I did not speak."

source_text: σχὼν κατὰ διάνοιαν τάραχόν τινα ἢ ἐν λογισμοῖς καὶ μηδὲν ἐνεργήσας κατὰ τὴν ταραχὴν τῶν λογισμῶν μηδὲ εἰπών, ἔχει τὸ τεταράχθαι καὶ μὴ λελαληκέναι. ὁ τοιοῦτος ἐντὸς ἔχ̣ει τὴν καρδίαν τεθερμανμ̣ένην. 4 καὶ ἐν τῇ μελέτῃ μου ἐκκαυθήσεται πῦρ. τὸ ἐντός μου. καὶ οὕτω καθ' ἕκ̣αστ̣ον ἡμῶν ἄνθρωποι δύο συνεστήκασιν, ὧν ὁ μὲν ἔξω, ὁ δὲ ἔσω. ὅταν τοίνυν ταραχὴ γένηται τῇ ψυχῇ καὶ μὴ ἐπὶ τὸν ἔξω ἄνθρωπον τὴν ταραχὴν μεταγάγῃ, ἀλλὰ τηρήσῃ αὐτὴν ἔνδον ὥστε καταγνῶναι αὐτῆς καὶ ἀποδακρύσασθαι αὐτήν, ἐντὸς ἔχει τὴν καρδίαν θερμανθεῖσαν, οὐχ ἵνα πράξῃ, ἀλλ' ἵνα μὴ πράξῃ. ἐν τῇ ἐμῇ μελέτῃ ἐκκαίεται τὸ πῦρ. ἐν τῇ ἄλλ̣ων φωνῇ καὶ πράξει καὶ διανοίᾳ ἐκκαίεται πῦρ ψαῦον αὐτῶν, πυροῦν αὐτούς. "ἀνεκαύθη ἡ καρδία αὐτῶν ὡς κλίβανος πυρός". ὧδε ἡ μελέτη ὡς πῦρ ἐξεκάη ἔχουσα ὕλην ὑποκειμένην καυστήν. ἡ δὲ μελέτη καὶ ἡ θέρμη τοῦ ἁγίου ἡ δ̣ιάπυρος, ἡ γινομένη ὑπὸ τοῦ ζέοντος πνεύματος. ἐκκαίεται οὖν τὸ πῦρ, ἵν' ἐνεργήσῃ τι, οὐχ ἵνα βλάψῃ καὶ ἀναλώσῃ. "οὐχὶ ἡ καρδία ἡμῶν ἦν καιομένη ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ, ἡνίκα διήνοιγεν ἡμῖν τὰς γραφάς"; ἡ καῦσις αὕτη ἐπαινετή ἐστιν. καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν τεχνητῶν δὲ σκόπει· ἔνια θερμαίνεται, ἵνα μεταρυθμισθῇ καὶ εἰς σκεῦος μεταβῇ, χρυσός, ἄργυρος. ἐὰν δὲ πυρωθῇ ξύλα ἠ`̣ ἄλλο τι, ἡ θέρμη βλαβερά ἐστιν. 4 ἐλάλησα ἐν γλώσσῃ. εἰ καὶ οὐκ ἔασα αὐτὴν ἔξω γενέσθαι, ἀλλ' ἐντός μου μείνασα πύρωσιν ἐκ μελέτης μοι περιεποιήσατο, τῇ δὲ γλώττῃ ἐλάλησα λοιπόν· "γνώρισόν μοι, κύριε, τὸ πέρας μου". ἀπὸ γλώττης τῆς ἐμῆς εἶπον τοῦτο· γλῶσσα γὰρ ἡ κατὰ φύσιν τοῦ ἔχοντος αὕτη ἐστίν· οἷον ὁ σώφρων τὰ σωφροσύνης λαλῶν ἐν γλώττῃ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ λαλεῖ, τοῦ σώφρονος, οὐκ ἐν γλώττῃ τοῦ ἀν θρώπου. καὶ ὁ θηρῶν μὲν τὸ πέρας ἑαυτοῦ μαθεῖν καὶ τῷ θεῷ προσάγων τὴν πεῦσιν, τῇ ἐμῇ γλώττῃ, οὐ τῇ δολίου ἀνθρώπου, ἀλλ' ἐμοῦ τοῦ θέλοντος γνῶναι τὸ πέρας μου ἐν γλώττῃ ἐλάλησα. ὁ λόγος μου οὗτος οὐκ ἐπίπλαστός ἐστιν. ὅταν τις ὑποκριτὴς λέγῃ περὶ σωφροσύνης οὐκ ὢν σώφρων, οὐ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ γλώττῃ λαλεῖ. ὁ δὲ σώφρων ὅτε περὶ σωφροσύνης διεξέρχεται λόγους, τῇ τοῦ σώφρονος γλώττῃ λαλεῖ. οὐδεὶς οὖν ὑποκριτὴς τῇ κατὰ φύσιν γλώττῃ λαλεῖ, ἀλλὰ τῇ ἐπιπλάστῳ. ὁ λύκος ὅτε δορὰν περικείμενος προβάτου πρόσεισιν τῇ Χριστοῦ ποίμνῃ, λαλεῖ οὐ τῇ γλώττῃ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ, ἀλλὰ μιμεῖται τὴν τοῦ προβάτου φωνήν, ἵν' ὡς ὅμοιος ὁμοίοις συντυχὼν βλάψῃ. 5 γνώρισόν μοι, κύριε, τὸ πέρας μου καὶ τὸν ἀριθμὸν τῶν ἡμερῶν μου, τίς ἐστιν. θεώρει ὡς μετανοοῦντός ἐστιν πρόσωπον τὸ ταῦτα λέγον. παρέστη μοι φυλάξαι τὰς ὁδούς μου, θεῖναι τῷ 185 στόματί μου φυλακήν. συνστάντος τοῦ ἁμαρτωλοῦ κατεναντίον μου καὶ ἐρεθίζοντος, ἀγαθὰ ἔλαβον ἐν διανοίᾳ τὰ πείσαντά με μὴ λαλῆσαι αὐτῷ. τοῦτο οὖν λέγω· ἐπεὶ πολλῶν ἐμαυτὸν ἐθεώρησα λειπόμενον–μόλις γὰρ ἠρξάμην προκοπῆς̣–, "γνώρισόν μοι, κύριε, τὸ πέρας μου", ἵνα γνῶ, πόσος μοι λείπεται χρόνος τῆς ζωῆς, εἰ αὐτάρκης ἐστὶν π̣ρὸς τὸ τελειωθῆναι καὶ πληρωθῆναι. οὕτω γοῦν καὶ ἄλλος ἔλεγεν· "τὴν ὀλιγότητα τῶν ἡμερῶν ἀπάγγειλόν μοι· μὴ ἀναγάγῃς με ἐν ἡμίσει ἡμε ρῶν μου". τρόπον τινὰ ἐν τῇ ἡμισείᾳ̣ τῶν ἡμερῶν τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ ἁγίου φωτὸς γινομένων εἰμί. μή με οὖν ἀναγάγῃς οὕτως. πλήρωσον οὖν τὰς ἡμέρας μου. πληροῖ δὲ ὁ θεὸς τάς τινων ἡμέρας οὐκ αὔξησιν αὐτῶν παρέχων· ὅταν γὰρ λέγῃ ὅτι· "μακρότητι ἡμερῶν ἐνπλήσω αὐτὸν" περὶ τοῦ δικαίου, οὐ τοῦτο λέγομεν ὅτι πολυετῆν αὐτὸν ποιεῖ. εἰσὶν καὶ ἀσεβεῖς πολλὰ ἔτη ζήσαντες. "καὶ τὸν ἀριθμὸν τῶν ἡμερῶν μου". δύναται καὶ "τὸν ἀριθμὸν τῶν ἡμερῶν μου" εἰπεῖν ὅτι· πολλά με ἐφώτισας, ἐν ἡμέραις γέγονα· ἕκαστος γὰρ φωτισμὸς ἡμέρα ἐστι´̣ν. τὸν ἀριθμὸν οὖν τῶν φωτισμῶν μου δήλω275 σόν μοι, ἵνα γνῶ, τί μοι λείπει. ὡς εἰ ἔλεγέν τις πόθον λαβὼν τέχνης ἢ ἐπιστήμης, μήπω δὲ τελείαν γνῶσιν ἐσχηκὼς τῆς παιδεύσεως–λέγει· "φανέρωσόν μοι, τίνα ἐστὶν τὰ φωτεινὰ τῆς ἐπιστήμης, ἵνα γνῶ, ποῖα ἔχω καὶ ποῖα λείπομαι". μακάριόν ἐστιν τὸ ἀριθμητὰ ἔχειν πράγματα καὶ ἔργα καὶ νοήματα, τὰ ἄξια τοῦ ἀριθμεῖσθαι. ἀμέλει γοῦν περὶ τῆς πόρνης λέγεται· "ἀναρίθμητοί εἰσιν, οὓς πεφόνευκας". οὐ τοῦτο λέγει πάντως ὅτι ἄπειροί εἰσιν, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἄξιοι τοῦ ἀριθμεῖσθαι. ἐν οὐδενὶ λόγῳ ἢ ἀριθμῷ κεῖνται. 5 ἵνα γνῶ τί ὑστερῶ ἐγώ. ἐὰν μάθω τὸν ἀριθμὸν τῶν ἡμερῶν μου καὶ τὸ πέρας μου, μέχρι πότε̣ παραγίνεται, γιγνώσκω, ἐν τίσιν ὑστερῶ, τίνα ἐστὶν ἃ οὔπω ἔμαθον. οἱ πόθον οὖν ἐνποιοῦντες ἐπιστή μης
english: Having experienced a disturbance in thought or in reasoning, and having done nothing according to that disturbance of thoughts, nor even having spoken, he possesses the state of having been disturbed and not having spoken. Such a person has within him a heart having been warmed. 'And in my meditation fire shall be kindled' (Ps 39:16). My inner self. And thus for each of us, two men have stood, the one outside, the other inside. Therefore, when a disturbance arises in the soul and does not transfer the disturbance to the outer man, but keeps it within so as to recognize it and weep over it, he has within him a heart having been warmed, not in order to act, but in order not to act. 'In my meditation the fire burns.' In others, by voice and by action and by thought, a fire burns, consuming them, burning them. 'Their heart was warmed like a fiery furnace.' Here the meditation is like a fire that has burned, having a combustible material lying beneath. And the meditation and the heat of the Holy [Spirit] is the all-consuming, which comes to pass by the blowing Spirit. Therefore the fire burns in order that it may act, not in order that it may harm and consume. 'Was not our heart burning within us while he opened to us the Scriptures?' (Lk 24:32). This burning is to be praised. And observe also regarding manufactured things: some are heated in order that they may be reshaped and become a vessel, gold or silver. But if wood or something else is set on fire, the heat is harmful.

'I spoke in a tongue.' Even if I did not let it become outward, but it remained within me, through a burning from meditation it made itself for me, and so I spoke in a tongue: 'Make known to me, Lord, my end' (Ps 62:5). From my own tongue I said this; for the tongue according to the nature of the possessor is this: for example, the temperate man, speaking the things of temperance, speaks in his own tongue, the tongue of the temperate man, not in the tongue of a human [deceiver]. And the one desiring to learn his own end and to offer his life to God, in my tongue, not in the tongue of a deceitful man, but I, desiring to know my end, spoke in a tongue. This my word is not a counterfeit. When a hypocrite speaks concerning temperance while not being temperate, he does not speak in his own tongue. But the temperate man, when he delivers discourses concerning temperance, speaks in the tongue of the temperate man. No hypocrite, therefore, speaks in the natural tongue, but in the counterfeit tongue. The wolf, when he [is...]

Begging like a sheep to enter Christ's flock, he speaks not in his own tongue, but imitates the voice of the sheep, so that, meeting like with like, he might harm. 'Make known to me, Lord, my end and the number of my days, what it is' (Psalm 39:10). Observe how the one saying this is a repentant person. 'Help me to guard my ways, to set a guard over my mouth' (Psalm 39:11-12). When the sinner stood against me and was provoking, I received good in my mind from the experience of not speaking to him.

This is therefore what I say; since I saw myself lacking much—for I had only just begun to progress—'Make known to me, Lord, my end,' so that I might know how much time of life remains to me, if it is sufficient for completion and fulfillment. Thus also another was saying: 'Declare to me the brevity of my days; do not bring me back in the midst of my days' (Psalm 39:13). In a certain way, I am in the midst of the days that come from the Holy Light. Do not then bring me back in such a way. Therefore, fulfill my days.

But God fulfills the days of some not by providing an increase of them; for when it is said, 'I will fill him with length of days' concerning the righteous, we do not say that he makes him many-years. There are also impious people who have lived many years. 'And the number of my days' (Psalm 39:10). It is also possible to say 'the number of my days' meaning: you have enlightened me much, I have become [composed of] days; for each enlightenment is a day. Therefore, reveal to me the number of my enlightenments, so that I might know what I lack.

As if someone, having taken up a desire for art or science, lest he should have a perfect knowledge of his education, says: 'Reveal to me what are the luminous things of science, so that I might know what I have and what I lack.' It is blessed to have things, works, and thoughts that are countable, those worthy of being numbered. Regarding the prostitute, it is indeed said: 'They are countless, whom you have slain' (Hosea 13:9). This does not necessarily mean that they are infinite, but that they are not worthy of being numbered. They do not exist in any word or number. So that I might know what I lack. If I learn the number of my days and my end, until when it is reached, I recognize in what things I lack, which are the things I have not yet learned. Therefore, those making a desire for science...

source_text: ὁλοσχερέσ̣τερον ἅμα τῷ ἄρξασθαι λέγουσιν αὐτοῖς τὰ θεωρήματα τὰ καταληφθέντα αὐτοῖς, ἵνα καὶ γνῶσιν, ὅσων λείπονται, καὶ πόθον λάβωσιν τοῦ κατορθῶσαι καὶ ἀναλαβεῖν. 6 ἰδοὺ παλαιστὰς ἔθου τὰς ἡμέρας μου. ἡ προτέρα ἀνάγνωσις ἡ δ̣ημωδεστέρα αὕτη ἐστίν· "παλαιὰς ἔθου τὰς ἡμέρας μου". οὔκ εἰμι νέος ἢ νεοπαγής, οὐ νῦν τοῦ ζῆν ἀρξάμενος, ἀλλὰ "παλαιὰς ἔθου τὰς ἡμέρας μου". καὶ τοῦτο δὲ ῥητέον· ἀεὶ τὸ ἐπερχόμενον παλαιοῖ τὸ φθάσαν. οὕτω γοῦν νόμοι παλαιου῀̣νται. τοῦτο οὖν λέγει· τὰς παλαιὰς ἃς εἶχον ἡμέρας, ὅτε κατὰ τὸν παλαιὸν ἔζων ἄνθρωπον, πεπαλαίωνται, ἀπῆλθαν· τὸν νέον ἐνεδυσάμην. ὁ μέντοι πρόχειρος ἐρεῖ ὅτι· "ἰδοὺ γέρων γέγονα. γνώρισόν μοι τὸ πέρας, πότε ἀποθνῄσκω". "ἰδοὺ παλαιςτὰς ἔθου τὰς ἡμέρας μου". ἐπεὶ ὁμώνυμόν ἐστιν τὸ ὄνομα τὸ "παλαιστής"–σημαίνει δὲ καὶ τὸν α᾿̣θλοῦντα ἐν πάλῃ, δηλοῖ δὲ καὶ μέτρον τι–, ἀμφοτέρως αὐτὸ ἐκλαβεῖν ἔστιν. λέγει ὅτι· "τὰς ἡμέρας μου ἐν πάλῃ κ̣αι`̣ ἀγω̣νίζεσθαι ἔθου"· ἀεὶ γὰρ ἔχομεν τοὺς πολεμοῦντας. καὶ ὁτὲ μὲν πειρασμὸς ἀνθρώπινος λαμβάνει καὶ τὰ ἀνθρώπινα πάθη πολεμεῖ καὶ παλαίει, ποτὲ πονηραὶ δυνάμεις· "οὐκ ἔστιν" γὰρ "ἡμῖν ἡ πάλη πρὸς αἷμα καὶ σάρκα"–ἡμῖν, ἄλλοις δὲ ναί–, "ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἀρχάς, πρὸς τὰς ἐξουσίας". ἵνα ᾖ τοῦτο, "ἀγῶνας ἔθου τὰς ἡμέρας μου". δύναται δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ μέτρου λεχθῆναι· ὡς πρὸς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος αἱ ἡμέραι ἃς ζῶ, παλαιστοῦ λόγον ἐπέχουσιν. καὶ ὥσπερ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη λέγει πολλὰ ὄντα "σταγόνα ἀπὸ κάδου"–ὡς πρὸς τὸν κάδον τῶν λογικῶν σταγὼν ὅλα τὰ ἔθνη εἰσίν–καὶ "ῥοπὴν ζυγοῦ"–μέχρι τοῦ ῥέψαι καταταλαντεύει τὸ βάρος, οὐχ ὥστε κάτω καθελκύσαι τὴν πλάστινγα–, ὡς πρὸς τὸ μέγεθος τῶν παλαἰώνων καὶ τὴν μακρότητα τῶν ἡμερῶν, ἣν ὑφίσταται ὁ δυνάμενος εὖ διάγειν· "ὁ φιλῶν", λέγει, "τὸν πατέρα καὶ τὴν μητέρα μακροχρόνιος ἔσται". καὶ οὐκ ἤδη κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν τοῦτο εὑρίσκεται. 6 καὶ ἡ ὑπόστασίς μου ὡσεὶ οὐδὲν ἐναντίον σου. τὸ τῆς ὑποστάσεως ὄνομα πολλὰ σημαίνει. ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος δὲ δύο σημαινομένων χρεία. λέγεταί ποτε ἡ οὐσία ὑπόστασις· ὡς ὅταν λέγηται ὁ υἱὸς 186 "χαρακτὴρ τῆς θεοῦ ὑποστάσεως", τῆς θεοῦ οὐσίας καὶ ὑπάρξεως. λέγεται δὲ ὑπόστασις καὶ ἡ τελεία ὑπομονὴ καθ' ἣν ὑφίσταταί τις τὰ ἐπίπονα. λέγει οὖν ἀμφοτέρως· "ἡ οὐσία τῆς ψυχῆς μου ἐναντίον σου ὡς οὐδέν ἐστιν", ὡς πρὸς σὲ μεγάλην τινὰ οὐσίαν. καὶ ὀφείλουσα εἶναι τελεία κατὰ σὲ τὸν πατέρα, ἠλάττωσα αὐτήν. καὶ ὅτι τοῦτο οὕτως ἔχει, λέγει περί τινων· "υἱοὶ Σιὼν οἱ τίμιοι οἱ ἐπηρμένοι χρυσίῳ καὶ ἀργυρίῳ πῶς ἐγενήθησαν εἰς ἀγγεῖα ὀστράκινα"; ἰδοὺ ἠλαττώθη αὐτῶν ἡ οὐσία. νοητῶς δε̣ι῀̣ τ̣ου῀̣τ̣ο λ̣αβεῖν· ὀστράκινα σκεύη γεγένηνται. λοιδορούμενον τὸ χρυσίον ἐλαττοῦται καὶ τῆς τιμῆς ἑαυτοῦ πολὺ ἀπολείπεται. ὁ μὴ συ̣νιεὶς τὴν προσοῦσαν αὐτῷ τιμὴν θεόθεν, "συνπαραβάλλεται τοῖς κτήνεσιν τοῖς ἀνοήτοις", καὶ ἡ ὑπόστασις αὐτοῦ δι' εὐτέλε̣ι̣αν οὐδὲν ἐνομίσθη. ἐπειδὴ δὲ καὶ τὴν ὑπομονὴν σημαίνει, λέγει ὅτι· εἰ καὶ ὑπέμεινα ποθῶν ἰδεῖν τὸ πέρας μου καὶ παρακαλῶ ἵνα γνωρίσῃς μοι τοῦτο, ἀλλ' οὐ῀̣ν γε ἡ ὑπομονή μου αὕτη ἡ οὕτως ὡς πρὸς σὲ βραχεῖά τίς ἐστιν. 6 πλὴν τὰ σύνπαντα ματαιότης, πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ζῶν. διχῶς τοῦτο γνῶναι δεῖ· τὰ μὲν πάντα τὰ διὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπον ματαιότης ἐστίν, ὡς ἀρτίως ἑρμήνευσεν ὁ ἐκκλησιαστής. πρὸς τὰ ὑπεραναβεβηκότα καὶ τέλεια̣ καὶ τὰ ἀληθῶς αἰώνια ἡ ὑπόστασις ματαία ἐστίν, πλὴν "πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ζῶν". οὕτω οὖν 276 δυνατὸν εἰπεῖν· καὶ ἂν π̣άντα ματαιότης ἐστὶν τὰ ἄλλα παρὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπον, οἷον τὰ θνητὰ ζῷα, τὰ πρόσκαιρα, καὶ ἂν ἄψυχα ὦσιν, ἀλλ' ὁ ἄνθρωπος μόνος ζῶν ἐστιν, ζῶν κατὰ τὴν ζωὴν ἐκείνην ἣν ζῶσιν κατὰ τὸν Ἀβραάμ· "οὐκ ἔστιν" γὰρ "ὁ θεὸς νεκρῶν, ἀλλὰ ζώντων". καὶ ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ ζῶν κατὰ τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην καὶ αὐτὸς μάταιός ἐστιν. διαστατέον οὖν οὕτως· τάδε πάντα ματαιότης ἐστίν̣· κἂν γὰρ θνητὰ ὦσιν, τεθνηκότα
english: More completely, they say the insights grasped by them are to be taught at the same time as the beginning, so that they may also know what they lack, and take up a desire to succeed and recover.

"Behold, I have made my days into wrestling matches." The former reading, this more common one, is: "I have made my days into old wrestling matches." I am not young or a newborn, not having begun to live just now, but "I have made my days into old wrestling matches." And this must be said: that which approaches always makes old that which has passed. Thus also laws grow old. Therefore he says: the old days which I had, when I lived as a man of old, have grown old and have departed; I have clothed myself in the new. But the one at hand will say: "Behold, I have become an old man. Make known to me the end, when I shall die." "Behold, I have made my days into wrestling matches." Since the name "wrestler" is homonymous—meaning also the one contending in the arena, and also indicating a certain measure—it is possible to take it both ways. He says: "I have made my days into wrestling in the arena"; for we always have those who fight against us. At times human temptation comes and fights and wears out human passions, and at other times evil powers; for "our wrestling is not against blood and flesh"—for us, but for others, yes—"but against the principalities, against the powers" (Ephesians 6:12). In order that this may be, "I have made my days into wrestling matches." And it can also be said by measure: as toward the age of the ages, the days which I live hold the character of a wrestler. And just as he says that all the nations are many things, "a drop from a bucket"—as toward the bucket of rational drops all the nations are—and "a weight on a scale"—until the weight tips and oscillates, not so as to pull the scale plate down—as toward the magnitude of the aging and the length of the days, which the one capable of living well endures: "the one loving" (Exodus 20:12) "his father and his mother shall be long-lived." And this is not yet found according to the literal word.

The name of hypostasis signifies many things. Regarding the present, there is a need for two meanings. Sometimes essence is called hypostasis; for instance, when the Son is called the 'character of the divine hypostasis' (cf. Heb 1:3), meaning the divine essence and existence. Hypostasis is also called perfect endurance, by which someone stands firm against hardships.

Thus he speaks in both senses: 'the essence of my soul is nothing before you' (Ps 51:6), as if toward you a certain great essence. And [saying] that it ought to be perfect according to you, the Father, I diminished it. And that this is so, he says concerning some: 'Children of Zion, the honored, adorned with gold and silver, how they became earthen vessels?' (2 Tim 2:20). Behold, their essence was diminished. It is clearly necessary to take this: they have become earthen vessels. The gold, being reviled, is diminished and falls far short of its own value. He who does not realize the honor coming to him from God 'is compared to the mindless cattle' (Ps 49:20), and his hypostasis, through poverty, was considered nothing.

And since it also signifies endurance, he says: even if I endured desiring to see my end and I entreat you that you make this known to me, yet my endurance is not something brief in this way toward you. Moreover, all things are vanity, every living man (Eccl 1:2). This must be known in two ways: all things are vanity through man, as the Preacher has clearly interpreted. Regarding the things that have ascended above and are perfect and truly eternal, the hypostasis is vain, except 'every living man.'

Thus it is possible to say: even if all other things apart from man are vanity, such as mortal animals, the transient things, even if they are soulless, man alone is living, living according to that life which they live according to Abraham; for 'God is not of the dead, but of the living' (Mk 12:27). And the man who lives according to the human [standard] is himself vain. Therefore, it must be distinguished thus: all these things are vanity; for even if they were mortal, having died.

source_text: οὐκέτι εἰσίν. ὁ δὲ ἄνθρωπος ζῶν ἐστιν. κἂν ἀποθάνῃ δέ, ἔτι ζῇ. ἢ οὕτως· ζῶν ἄνθρωπος ο῾̣ μὴ ἔξω γινόμενος τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης ζωῆς καὶ αὐτὸς ματαιότης ἐστίν, ἵν' ᾖν οὖν οὕτως· "πλὴν τὰ σύνπαντα ματαιότης καὶ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ζῶν". ἢ οὕτως· "πλὴν τὰ σύνπαντα ματαιότης, ὁ δὲ ἄνθρωπος ζῶν ἐστιν". ἐπερ · ἡ οὐσία; –κἂν ζῇ ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἑτέρως ἢ ὡς ἂν ζήσαιεν θνητός, ὡς πρὸς τὴν ὑπεροχὴν καὶ τὸ μέγεθος τῆς θείας ζωῆς καὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ, τῆς πηγῆς τῆς ζωῆς, οὐθέν ἐστιν. τὰ μικρὰ καὶ τὰ οὐθὲν μικρότερα λεγόμενα τ̣ῶν πρός τί ἐστιν. οὐκ ἔχει δὲ περιωρισμένον ποσὸν τὸ μικρόν· ἀναφορᾷ γὰρ τῇς πρὸς τὸ μεῖζον λέγεται. λέγομεν οὖν μεῖζον ἐνίοτε τὸ παλαιστιαῖον τοῦ δακτυλιαίου. ἀμέλει γοῦν ἔχεις ἐν κατηγορίαις μικρὸν ὄρος καὶ μεγάλην κέγχρον. 7 μέντοιγε ἐν εἰκόνι διαπορεύεται ἄνθρωπος. εἶπον ὅτι περὶ τῶν ἄλλων παρὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπον λέγει, ὅτι "πάντα ματαιότης ἐστίν". μόνος ο῾̣ ἄνθρωπος ζῶν ἐστιν. ἔχει δὲ πλέον τι τῶν ἄλλων. ἀθάνατον ψυχὴν ἔχει. ὅμως εἰ καὶ ζῶν ἐστιν, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἀεὶ ταύτην τὴν κ̣ίνησιν ἔχει· "μέντοιγε", γάρ, φησίν, "ἐν εἰκόνι διαπορεύεται ἄνθρωπος". οὐκ εἶπεν εἰ ἐπαινετῇ ἢ ψεκτῇ· ἀλλ' οἵως ἐάν τις διαπορεύηται, οἵως ἐὰν ἐνεργῇ, ἐν εἰκόνι τινί ἐστιν. καὶ γενικώτερον λαμβάνοντι λεκτέον, ὅτι ἢ τῇ τοῦ ἐπουρανίου ἢ τῇ τοῦ χοικοῦ. παρίσταται δὲ ἐκ τῆς τοιαύτης λέξεως ὅτι αὐτεξούσιός ἐστιν ὁ ἄνθρωπος· εἰ γὰρ ἐκ κατασκευῆς ἦν ἀγαθός, ἐν τῇ τοῦ ἐπουρανίου ἀεὶ ἐπορεύετο, εἰ κατ' οὐσίαν ἦν κακός, ἐν τῇ τοῦ χοικοῦ. δυνατὸν δὲ ταύτας τὰς γενικὰς εἰκόνας εἰς εἴδη διαιρῆσαι. καὶ λέγω ὅτι ὁ μὲν ἐν εἰκόνι ἀλώπεκος, ἄλλος ἐν εἰκόνι λέοντος, καὶ ἵππος θηλυμανής τις γινόμενος ἄλλην φέρων εἰκόνα, καὶ ἕτερος ἐν εἰκόνι περιστερᾶς, πλὴν "ἐν εἰκόνι διαπορεύεται πᾶς ἄνθρωπος". 7 μέντοιγε ἐν εἰκόνι διαπορεύεται ἄνθρωπος, πλὴν μάτην ταράσσονται. ἀλλ' οἱ φαῦλοι μάτην ταράσσονται. "πλὴν μάτην ταράσσονται". καὶ λέγει λοιπὸν τὴν ταραχὴν τὴν ματαίαν, ὅτι ἡ περὶ τὰ ἀνθρώπινα σπουδὴ αὕτη ἐστίν. "θησαυρίζει" γοῦν "καὶ οὐ γιγνώσκει τίνι συνάγει αὐτά". 7 θησαυρίζει καὶ οὐ γιγνώσκει τίνι συνάγει αὐτά. ἐν τῷ ἐκκλησιαστῇ φανερῶς ἐλέχθη ὅτι· "οὐκ οἶδεν εἰ σοφὸς ἔσται" ὁ 187 διάδοχος τῶν ὑπαρχόντων αὐτοῦ "ἢ ἄφρων". καὶ πολλάκις ἃ ἐθησαύρισέν τις, καταλιμπάνει. ἐνίοτε δὲ καὶ ἐνιαυτοῦ περιόντος εἰς ἄλλους ἐκεῖνα μεταπίπτει. διὸ οὐ δεῖ σπουδάζειν περὶ τὸ οὕτω θησαυρίζειν· "οὐκ ὠφελήσουσιν" γὰρ "θησαυροὶ ἀνόμους, δικαιοσύνη δὲ ῥύεται ἐκ θανάτου". δικαιοσύνην ἄρα τὴν ῥυομένην ἐκ θανάτου καὶ παντὸς ἄλλου κακοῦ θησαυριστέον. θησαυρίζεται δὲ ἐν οὐρανῷ ὁ πλοῦτος οὗτος. "μὴ θησαυρίζετε ὑμῖν θησαυροὺς ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ἀλλὰ θησαυρίζετε θησαυροὺς ἐν οὐρανῷ"· ἐπεὶ γὰρ ὅπου ὁ θησαυρός, ἐκεῖ καὶ ὁ νοῦς ἐστιν "καρδία" ὀνομαζόμενος, ἐν οὐρανῷ θησαυριστέον, ἵν' ἐκεῖ τὸν νοῦν ἔχωμεν, καὶ παραιτητέον ἐν τῇ γῇ θησαυρίζειν, ἵνα μὴ ἐκεῖ τὴν διάνοιαν σχῶμεν. λέγεται περί τινων· "οἱ θησαυρίζοντες ἀδικίαν καὶ ταλαιπωρίαν ἐν ταῖς χώραις αὐτῶν". ὁ ἐν εἰκόνι οὖν διαπορευόμενος ἄνθρωπος θησαυρίζων οὐκ οἶδεν τίνι συνάγει αὐτά· ἄδηλον γάρ ἐστιν αὐτῷ ὅ, τι μετελεύσεται. διὸ ὁ σπουδαῖος ἀκούει θησαυρίζειν ἐν οὐρανοῖς. ἔχει ἀποκείμενον τὸν πλοῦτον ἐν ἔργοις ἀγαθοῖς. τοῦτό τοι καὶ Παῦλος ἐπιστέλλει Τιμοθέῳ· "τοῖς πλουσίοις τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου παράγγελλε μὴ ὑψηλὰ φρονεῖν ἐπὶ πλούτῳ, ἀλλὰ ἐπὶ τῷ θεῷ τῷ παρέχοντι πάντα". λεκτέον καὶ περὶ ψεκτοῦ πλούτου, οἷον τῆς αἱρεθικῆς γνώμης τῶν δογμάτων τῶν ἀθέων. καὶ ὁ ταῦτα θησαυρίζων οὐκ οἶδεν τίνι συνάγει αὐτά. ἄλλῳ δὲ αὐτὸν καταλιμπάνει· μέχρι γὰρ τῆς παρούσης ζωῆς ἔχει τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν "ἡ ψευδώνυμος 277 γνῶσις"· ἐπιλαμψάσης γὰρ τῆς ἀληθείας λύεται καὶ ἀφανίζεται. ἐπερ · "μέντοιγε ἐν εἰκόνι"; –εἰ καὶ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ζῶν ἐστιν, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἀπαραβάτως ἐν τῷ ζῆν τῷ ἐπαινετῷ ἐστιν· εἰ γὰρ ἔμενεν ἐν τῇ ἀληθινῇ εἰκόνι τῇ πρώτῃ καθ' ἣν ἐδημιουργήθη, οὐκ ἐταράττετο, οὐ μάτην ἐθησαύριζεν. μέντοιγε, εἰ καὶ γέγονεν ζῶν, ἐν εἰκόνι διαπορεύεται· οὐ πάντως δὲ τῇ πρώτῃ, ἀλλὰ ἁπαξαπλῶς ἐν εἰκόνι· οὐδέποτε γὰρ τὸ λογικὸν ζῷον δύναται ἔξω τοῦ κατὰ λόγον ἐνεργεῖν γενέσθαι. ἐνεργῶν δὲ πάντως ἢ ἐπαινετῶς ἢ ψεκτῶς ἐνεργεῖ, καὶ τάδε τινὰ φρονῶν καὶ πράττων καὶ τάδε τινά. ἐπερ · "πλὴν μάτην ταράσσονται"; –πολλάκις ἤδη ἐλέχθη ἡμῖν ὅτι αἱ μεταβολα̣ὶ οὕτως γινόμεναι ἔχουσίν τινα διαφοράν. τότε ὅταν μὴ ταύτην τὴν εἰκόνα φυλάττωσιν καθ' ἣν γεγόνασιν, πλῆθός εἰσιν οἱ μάτην
english: They are no longer. But the man is living. Even if he should die, he still lives. Or in this way: a man living who does not become outside of human life is himself vanity; so that it is thus: 'except all things are vanity and every living man' (Eccl 1:2). Or in this way: 'except all things are vanity, but the man is living'. Beyond this: the essence? Even if the man lives differently than a mortal would live, in view of the excellence and the greatness of the divine life and of God himself, the fountain of life, he is nothing.

The small things and the things no smaller than small are said in relation to something. And the small does not have a limited amount; for it is said in reference to the greater. We say, for instance, that the wrestler is greater than the boxer. Indeed, you have in categories a small mountain and a large gulf. 'But indeed, a man wanders in an image' (Eccl 1:14). I said that he speaks about the others besides the man, saying that 'all is vanity'. Only the man is living. And he has more than the others. He has an immortal soul.

However, even if he is living, he does not always have this motion; 'but indeed', for he says, 'a man wanders in an image' (Eccl 1:14). He did not say whether he wanders in praise or in mockery; but however anyone wanders, however he acts, he is in some image. Taking it more generally, it is to be said that it is either of the heavenly or of the earthly. And it is shown from such a word that the man is self-determining; for if he were good by construction, he would always wander in the heavenly, if he were evil by essence, in the earthly.

And it is possible to divide these general images into kinds. And I say that one is in the image of a fox, another in the image of a lion, and a certain mare becoming a horse carrying another image, and another in the image of a dove, except 'in an image every man wanders'. 'But indeed, a man wanders in an image' (Eccl 1:14), except vainly they are troubled. But the worthless are vainly troubled. 'Except vainly they are troubled'. And he therefore speaks of the vain trouble, because this striving concerning human things is such. For instance, he 'stores up' 'and does not know to whom he gathers them' (Eccl 2:18). He stores up and does not know to whom he gathers them. In Ecclesiastes it was clearly said that: 'he does not know whether he will be wise' (Eccl 2:19), the successor of those who are.

His [words] 'or fools'. And often what one has treasured, he leaves behind. Sometimes, as a year passes, he falls away into other things. Therefore, it is not necessary to be anxious about treasuring in this way; for 'lawless treasures will not profit, but righteousness rescues from death' (Prov 11:4). Therefore, the righteousness that rescues from death and from every other evil is to be treasured. This wealth is treasured in heaven.

'Do not treasure for yourselves treasures on earth, but treasure treasures in heaven' (Matt 6:19-21); because where the treasure is, there also the mind is, which is called the 'heart'. It is to be treasured in heaven so that we may have the mind there, and one should refrain from treasuring on earth, so that we may not have the intellect there. It is said concerning some: 'those treasuring injustice and misery in their lands'.

The man, therefore, wandering in an image, treasuring, did not know to whom he was bringing them; for it is unclear to him what he will bequeath. Therefore, the diligent one hears to treasure in the heavens. He has wealth set aside in good works. This is also what Paul writes to Timothy: 'command the rich of this age not to be high-minded concerning wealth, but in God, who provides all things' (1 Tim 6:17).

It must also be said concerning false wealth, such as the heretical opinion of the dogmas of the atheists. And he who treasures these things did not know to whom he was bringing them. But he leaves them to another; for until the present life, he holds the promise of 'the pseudonymous knowledge' (1 Tim 6:20); for when the truth shines forth, it is dissolved and vanishes.

And what about 'only in an image'?—even if every man is living, he is not living without transgression in the praiseworthy living. For if he had remained in the true image, the first, according to which he was created, he would not have been troubled, nor would he have treasured in vain. But indeed, even if he has become living, he wanders in an image; and not altogether in the first, but rather wandering in an image; for never can the rational animal be able to act outside of acting according to reason. And acting, he acts either praiseworthily or falsely, thinking and doing certain things and certain others.

And what about 'but in vain they are troubled'?—it has often already been said to us that these changes occur in such a way. When they do not guard this image according to which they have become, they are a multitude of the vain.

source_text: ταραττόμενοι. ὅτε δὲ τὴν ζωὴν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου σημαίνει, ὅτι "πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ζῶν", καὶ "μέντοιγε ἐν εἰκόνι διαπορεύεται ἄνθρωπος"–οὐ τῇ αὐτῇ, ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ διάφοροί εἰσιν αἱ εἰκόνες, καὶ μάλιστα δὲ ψεκταὶ καὶ ὑποβεβηκυῖαι, πολλοί εἰσιν οἱ ταραττόμενοι. 8 καὶ νῦν τίς ἡ ὑπομονή μου; οὐχὶ κύριος; περὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἐλέχθη τὰ εἰρημένα. ἐγὼ δὲ περὶ ἐμαυτοῦ λέγω· "τίς ἡ ὑπομονή μου; οὐχὶ κύριος"; μὴ ἄλλον ὑπομένω. καὶ ὥσπερ "γίνεται σοφία καὶ δικαιοσύνη καὶ ἁγιασμὸς" τοῖς μετέχουσιν, οὕτω καὶ ὑπομονὴ γίνεται τῷ ὑπομένοντι αὐτὸς ὁ κύριος. 8 καὶ ἡ ὑπόστασίς μου παρὰ σοῦ ἐστιν. περὶ τοῦ κυρίου λέγει ὅτι ὑπομονὴ αὐτοῦ ἐστιν. πρὸς αὐτὸν δὲ τὸν κύριον τὸν ὄντα αὐτοῦ ὑπομονὴν λέγει· "καὶ ἡ ὑπόστασίς μου παρὰ σοῦ ἐστιν". δύναται ὑπόσ̣τασιν ἐνταῦθα λέγειν τὴν ἰσχὺν καθ' ἣν ὑποστῆναί τις δύναται, ὅτι σοῦ συνεργοῦντος καὶ ὄντος μου ὑπομονῆς ὑφίσταμαι π̣άντα. ἡ δὲ "παρὰ σοῦ ὑπόστασις" ἐπαινετή μοί ἐστιν. δυνατὸν δὲ ὑπόστασιν λέγειν ἀντὶ οὐσίας. καὶ ἡ ὑπόστασίς μου τῆς λογικῆς ψυχῆς, τοῦ λογικοῦ ζῴου παρὰ σοῦ ἐστιν· σὺ γὰρ δέδωκάς μοι ψυχήν, παρὰ σοῦ ἔχω τὴν ψυχὴν οὐκ ἀπὸ σπερμάτων ἀρχομένην, οὐ κατὰ ἔμφασιν συνισταμένην κατὰ τὴν Στρατιωτικὴν αἵρεσιν, ἀλλὰ "παρὰ σοῦ ἐστιν ἡ ὑπόστασίς μου". 9 ἀπὸ πασῶν τῶν ἀνομιῶν μου ῥῦσαί με. οὐκ ἀπὸ τινῶν, ἀλλὰ "ἀπὸ πασῶν", ἵνα πάσης εἰκόνος ἔξω ψεκτῆς γένωμαι. 9 ὄνειδος ἄφροσιν ἔδωκάς με. ἐξ ἀρχῆς εἴπομεν ὅτι μετανοῦντος καὶ προκόπτοντος πρόσωπον φέρει ὅλος ὁ ψαλμός. φαῦλον πρᾶγμά ἐστιν ὀνειδίζεσθαι ὑπὸ δικαίου, ὑπὸ δὲ ἄφρονος ἐπαινετόν. ὀνειδίζει γοῦν ἐπὶ ἀγαθοῖς ἔργοις καὶ ἐπὶ σπουδῇ ὁ ἄφρων. διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἐν παροιμίαις ὡς διαφορᾶς 188 οὔσης ὀνειδισμῶν λέγεται· "μὴ κτήσῃ κακῶν ἀνδρῶν ὀνείδη"· μὴ γὰρ εἶπεν καθόλου· "μὴ κτήσῃ ὀνείδη", ἀλλὰ "κακῶν ἀνδρῶν". μὴ ἐπὶ φαυλότητι ὀνειδίζου· εἰσὶν γὰρ ὀνειδιζόμενοι ἐπὶ καλοῖς. τοῖς γοῦν γνωρίμοις Ἰησοῦς λέγει· "χαίρετε καὶ ἀγαλλιᾶτε ὅταν ὀνειδίζωσιν ὑμᾶς". οὐ τοῦτον τὸν ὀνειδισμὸν παραιτητέον· ἀγαθὸς γάρ ἐστιν καὶ ξεναγεῖ εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν. τοὺς δὲ τῶν κακῶν ἀνδρῶν ὀνειδισμοὺς φευκτέον. 10 ἐκωφώθην καὶ οὐκ ἤνοιξα τὸ στόμα μου. τίς ἐστιν ὁ ὀνειδίζων ἄφρων ἢ ἐκεῖνος ὁ ἁμαρτωλὸς ὁ συνστὰς κατεναντίον αὐτοῦ, ὅσον "ἐκωφώθη καὶ οὐκ ἤνοιξεν τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ"; καὶ ἐνταῦθα πάλιν τὸ αὐτὸ σημαίνει· "ἐκωφώθην καὶ οὐκ ἤνοιξα τὸ στόμα μου". οὐκ ἀπεκρίθην αὐτῷ πρὸς ἃ ὀνειδίζει. ἔλεγον δὲ τοῦτο πολλάκις ὅτι ἄλλῃ δυνάμει ὁ ἀπόστολος τοῦτο διδάσκει λέγων· "αἱρεθικὸν ἄνθρωπον ἀπὸ μιᾶς νουθεσίας παραιτοῦ". μὴ ἄνοιγε αὐτῷ ὅλως τὸ στόμα. ὅπως δὲ ἂν ἀπολογητικὸν ἔχῃς καὶ σοὶ λόγον περὶ σεαυτοῦ εἰπεῖν ὅτι· "τὸ παρ' ἐμαυτοῦ πεποίηκα", νουθέτησον αὐτόν. ἐὰν τῆς νουθεσίας μὴ ἀνάςχηται ἢ "καὶ δευτέρας"–ἔνια γὰρ τῶν ἀντιγράφων ἔχει "καὶ δευτέρας"–, ἀνάτραπε αὐτὸν "εἰδὼς ὅτι ἁμαρτάνει". τὸν "αὐτοκατάκριτον" οὐ δεῖ νου θετεῖν. 10–11 ὅτι σὺ εἶ ὁ ποιήσας με, ἀπόστησον ἀπ' ἐμοῦ τὰς μάστιγάς σου. μὴ μάστιζέ με· ποίημα γὰρ σοῦ εἰμι. "μαστιγοῖ δὲ πάντα υἱὸν ὃν παραδέχεται" ἔχοντα δηλονότι δι' ἃ μαστίζεται. ταῦτα οὖν ἄφες μοι· ἄφεσιν μοι δώρησαι· οὕτω γὰρ οὐκέτι μαστιχθήσομαι. νῦν δ̣ε`̣ ἐ´̣τι υ῾̣πε̣υ´̣θυνος μάστιξίν εἰμι. 278 ἀμέλει γοῦν ὁ τὸν ὕψιστον θέμενος καταφυγὴν ἑαυτοῦ οὐκ ἔχει προσεγγίζοντα κακὰ οὐδὲ μάστιγαν ἐγγίζουσαν τοῦ σκηνώματος αὐτοῦ. ποίησόν με οὖν τοιοῦτον ὥστε μηκέτι ὑπεύθυνον εἶναι μάστιξιν, τὸ κ̣ολαστέον μου ἀπόστησον. ἐπεὶ τοίνυν λέγω ὅτι· "ἀπὸ πασῶν τῶν ἀνομιῶν μου ῥῦσαί με", ὅταν ῥύσῃ με, ου᾿̣κέτι κολαστέος εἰμί. τρόπον οὖν τινα ἐμάστιζεν αὐτὸν καὶ διὰ τοῦ ἄφρονος, καὶ λέγει τοὺς ὀνειδισμοὺς τοῦ ἄφρονος μάστιγας εἶναι. εἰ μὴ ὁ θεὸς παραδῷ, οὐκ ἰσχύει οὐδὲ ἐναντιούμενος τῷ μήπω παραδοθέντι. 11 ἀπὸ τῆς ἰσχύος τῆς χειρός σου ἐγὼ ἐξέλιπον. ἐπίκειταί μοι ἡ ἰσχὺς τῆς χειρός σου ἡ παιδευτική, ἡ πλήττουσα, ἡ πόνοις ὑποβάλλουσα. ἐπεὶ οὖν ἰσχυρὰ γέγονεν ἐπ' ἐμοί, ἐξέλιπον. ἀπέβαλον τὴν προτέραν μου ζωήν, ἀπέλιπον τὴν προτέραν κατάστασιν· οὐ γὰρ ἐξέλιπον ὥστε μηκέτι εἶναι, ὥστε ἀσθενὴς γενέσθαι, ἀλλ' ὥστε ἐκλιπεῖν τὴν κατάστασιν τὴν κολαστέον με παρασκευάζουσαν. "ἐγὼ ἐξέλιπον". ἐγὼ ὁ ταῦτα λέγων, ὁ ἐξομολογούμενος, ὁ λέγων· "ὄνειδος ἄφροσιν ἔδωκάς με", ἐξέλιπον ἔξω γενόμενος τῆς προτέρας μου καταστάσεως. ἔστιν ἐπαινετῶς ἐκλιπεῖν, ἔστιν δὲ καὶ ψεκτῶς. "ἦλθεν δὲ Ἠσαῦ ἐκ τοῦ πεδίου ἐκλείπων", ὅτε ἠθέλη̣σ̣εν ἕψημα φαγεῖν. τὸ ὧδε "ἐκλείπων" ἀντὶ τοῦ "ἀσθενήσας" καὶ "ὀρεγόμενος τροφῆς". λέγεται πολλάκις
english: They are being disturbed. When he signifies the life of man, he says, 'every man lives' (Ps 39:1), and 'yet a man wanders in an image'—not in the same one, but because the images are diverse, and especially because many are false and deceptive, many are being disturbed. And now, what is my stability? Is it not the Lord? Regarding others, the things spoken have been said. But as for myself, I say: 'What is my stability? Is it not the Lord?' (Ps 39:17) I do not wait for another. And just as 'wisdom, righteousness, and sanctification become' those who participate, so also stability becomes to the one waiting, the Lord himself. And my subsistence is with you. Concerning the Lord, he says that his stability is. But toward the Lord, who is, he says his subsistence is: 'and my subsistence is with you' (Ps 39:18). It is possible to call subsistence here the strength by which one is able to stand, because, with you cooperating and being my stability, I stand against all things. And the 'subsistence from you' is a praise to me. And it is possible to call subsistence instead of essence. And my subsistence of the rational soul, of the rational animal, is with you; for you have given me a soul; from you I have the soul, not beginning from seeds, not being composed according to an opinion like the Stoic school, but 'my subsistence is from you' (Ps 39:18).

Save me from all my lawlessness (Ps 39:19). Not from some, but 'from all,' so that I may become outside of every false image. A reproach of foolishness you have given me (Ps 39:20). From the beginning we said that the whole psalm bears the face of one repenting and progressing. It is a trivial thing to be reproached by a righteous man, but to be praised by a fool. For the fool indeed reproaches regarding good works and with zeal. For this reason, even in proverbs, as if there were no difference, reproaches are mentioned: 'Do not acquire the reproach of evil men' (Prov 22:8); for he did not say at all, 'Do not acquire reproach,' but 'of evil men.' Do not reproach regarding triviality; for there are those being reproached regarding good things. To the well-known, Jesus says: 'Rejoice and be glad when they reproach you' (Matt 5:11). This kind of reproach is not to be rejected; for it is good and will lead into the kingdom of heaven. But the reproaches of evil men are to be fled from. I was made mute and I did not open my mouth (Ps 39:21). Who is the foolish reproacher, or he is the sinner who stands against him, as...

"He became mute and did not open his mouth"? And here again the same thing is signified: "I became mute and did not open my mouth." He did not answer him regarding what he reproaches. This is often said by another power, as the apostle teaches this, saying: "Reprove not a contentious man for one exhortation" (Prov 9:8). Do not open the mouth to him at all. But so that you may have a defense and a word to say about yourself, "I have done this by myself," exhort him. If he does not submit to the exhortation, or "and a second"—for some manuscripts have "and a second"—overthrow him, "knowing that he sins." One who is "self-condemning" should not be set against.

10–11 For you are the one who made me, turn away your whips from me. Do not lash me; for I am your handiwork. "But he lashes every son whom he receives" (Heb 12:6), having it clear through which he is lashed. Therefore, leave these things to me; grant me a remission, for in this way I shall no longer be lashed. Now I am still liable for the lashings. 278 Therefore, he who has placed the Most High as his refuge (Ps 91:2) has no approaching evils nor a whip approaching his tent. Make me therefore such that I am no longer liable for the lashings; turn away the thing that punishes me. Since therefore I say, "Deliver me from all my iniquities" (Ps 51:2), when you deliver me, I am no longer liable for punishment.

He was lashing him in a certain way even through the thoughtless man, and says that the reproaches of the thoughtless are the lashes. Unless God delivers, one is not able even by opposing that which has not been delivered. 11 From the strength of your hand I have failed (Ps 31:9). The strength of your hand, the educational one, the striking one, the one subjecting to pains, presses upon me. Since therefore it has become strong against me, I have failed. I cast away my former life, I left my former state; for I did not fail so as to no longer exist, or to become weak, but so as to fail the state preparing to punish me. "I have failed." I, saying these things, confessing, saying, "You have given me reproach through thoughtlessness," have failed, having become outside of my former state. It is possible to fail praiseworthily, and it is possible to fail shamefully. "And Esau came from the field, leaving behind" (Gen 25:29), when he desired to eat a meal. The "leaving behind" here is instead of "having grown weak" and "longing for food." It is said often...

english: spiritual

If one attempts things that are different—and one is true and the other is false—one knows from the attempt at opposites which is true and which is false. Indeed, the true itself appears by the showing of the false, because knowledge is of the opposites.

"And you searched out his soul like a spider" (Ps 90:8). You searched out his soul like a spider, his soul according to which he is psychic. Concerning someone bad it is said, "he was carried by the desires of his soul." When someone reshapes [things] from the soul, let it be said, as if they were prophecies or as if they were doctrines of piety, "he is carried by the desires of the soul"; he is not carried by the Holy Spirit.

In another book I have stated the difference: that man is fleshly, he who fights according to the flesh, he who follows the desires of the flesh, he who is driven by the flesh, he who has become fleshly and is driven by sin. But a man is spiritual who has ascended above the psychic state, when he carries everything by the Holy Spirit and by God-bearing, doing and practicing [them]. And psychic is he who is neither fleshly nor spiritual.

And perhaps all the wise of the world are such. They think themselves self-sufficient according to the movements and thoughts of their own souls. And because of this they do not receive the things of the Spirit; for they prefer their own and think their own understanding to be great, they do not receive the foolishness of the Spirit, regarding it as such. And indeed there are certain heresies established in their entirety, both among the Greeks and among the Christians, which say that allegories are foolishnesses, they are mere fabrications. And they say that the theorems concerning the intelligible are false, since they think all things to be bodies and sensible.

These, therefore, are psychic men, not receiving the things of the Spirit, regarding themselves as self-sufficient and capable of contemplating all things by themselves. His soul, then, such a soul—not the essence, but the state according to which it is a soul—you searched out like a spider. And the spider is very weak, as it is said, "they weave a spider's web; their web shall not be a garment" (Job 8:14). The fragility of the construction of the animal...

"ἐλθάτω ἡ βασιλεία σου". ποίησον αὐτὴν ἐλθεῖν. τότε δὲ ἔρχεται, ὁ´̣τ̣αν κατ' ἐνέργειαν ἡμῶν ὁ θεὸς βασιλεύῃ. 13 ἐνώτισαι τῶν δακρύων μου. θεωρῶν ἐμαυτὸν ἐνλιπῆ δακρύω ποιω῀̣ν ἐκείνην καὶ κατασκευάζων "τὴν λύπην τὴν κατὰ θεὸν εἰς μετάνοιαν εἰς σωτηρίαν ἐργαζομένην" καθ' ἣν λέγω· "λούσω καθ' ἑκάστην νύκταν τὴν κλίνην μου, ἐν δάκρυσίν μου τὴν στρωμνήν μου βρέξω". ἐπειδὴ δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀπολειπόμενος τῆς τελείας καὶ ἄκρας ἀρετῆς–, πάλιν ὀλοφύρεται λέγων· "οἱ ὄντες ἐν τῷ σκήνει στενάζομεν", καὶ πάλιν· "ἔθου τὰ δάκρυά μου ἐναντίον σου ὡς ἐν τῇ ἐπαγγελίᾳ σου". θεωρεῖς· "ὡς ἐν τῇ ἐπαγγελίᾳ ἔθου τὰ δάκρυά μου". ποῖα δέ ἐστιν δάκρυα ἢ τὰ τῶν κλαιόντων, ἵνα γελάσωσιν; "μακάριοι" γὰρ "οἱ κλαίοντες νῦν ὅτι γελάσονται". οὗτοι ἔθεντο τὰ δάκρυα ὡς ἐν τῇ ἐπαγγελίᾳ, ἵνα γελάσωσιν, ἵνα πληρωθῶσιν "χαρᾶς
english: Regarding the one called a spider, he says there is an extension of the soul. When the soul is stretched out, this extension occurs for its own benefit; for the spider-like quality is weak in it, and moreover it is shown to be an external evil. Therefore, you have examined the soul of this man as a spider, he who is being reproved under accusations for lawlessness.

12 Moreover, every man is tossed about in vain. All men who are outside the instruction of God and the reproofs are tossed about in vain. But this one, even if he is tossed about while being reproved, even if his soul is stretched out like a spider, he does not suffer this in vain; for he receives a change toward better things. But if anyone were such a bare man, not being under instruction, not being under reproofs, he is tossed about in vain according to what was said previously: 'Indeed, man wanders in an image, but they are tossed about in vain' (Ps 94:11). He who does not wish to be tossed about, but has tranquility, becomes God, having received the word of God; for 'he called those gods, those to whom the word of God came' (Ps 82:6). And these are not tossed about in vain, but even if it happens that they slip or a passion occurs, they say: 'I was tossed about and I did not speak.' Their tossing stands only until passion.

Furthermore: do they toss about from themselves? — At times they toss about from themselves, at other times from those encountering them. 13 Hear, O Lord, my prayer and my supplication. It seems there is something else that is the supplication of the prayer. He sends up a supplication, the one who has known himself to be begging and lacking, so that he may be filled. But the one praying has this form as well, yet at times asks for the existence of good things from above. The one asking from God to receive something, that is, what he does not have, asks to receive it, or what he has, so that it may remain with him. Primarily this is prayer; it is a request sent up along with the one theologizing, the one wishing, to whom the prayer is sent up. When he says: 'Lord our God, give us peace, for you gave us all things' (Hab 3:2). 'The prayer of Habakkuk the prophet.'

He said: 'Lord, I have heard your voice and was astounded. Let him be known in the midst of two living creatures; when the years approach, he shall not be known' (Habakkuk 3:2). Behold, this is a prayer. When one asks for only those things which he lacks while being in need, it is a petition, being sent back like a wish. It is also possible to take it this way: those asking for more bodily things petition, such as health, wealth, and the others, as being in need, and many times they are worthy to receive these. But he who desires to have fullness, says: 'The prayer of Habakkuk the prophet: Lord, I have heard your voice and was astounded. Let him be known in the midst of two living creatures; when the years approach, he shall not be known' (Habakkuk 3:2). Behold, this is a prayer.

'Lord our God, give us peace, for you have given us all things' (1 Chronicles 29:14). Since even as one lacking, I ask that something might be given to me—for I am still at the peak of childhood—listen to my petition. But since I am about to come by chance to those things of which I am lacking, having become full, I ask for greater things; I ask for heavenly things and I say: 'Our Father who is in the heavens, hallowed be your name' (Matthew 6:9)—not as one lacking does he ask this. 'Let your kingdom come' (Matthew 6:10). Make it come. Then it comes, so that God may reign according to our energy.

Unite them with my tears. Seeing myself lacking, I weep, making that 'godly sorrow working repentance unto salvation' (2 Corinthians 7:10), regarding which I say: 'I will wash my bed every night, with my tears I will wet my couch.' And since he who is lacking perfection and the extremity of virtue—again he pours himself out saying: 'We who dwell in the tent groan' (Psalm 88:7), and again: 'I have poured out my tears before you according to your promise'—you see: 'as in the promise I have poured out my tears.' What tears are these, or those of the ones weeping so that they might laugh? For 'blessed' are 'those who weep now, that they may laugh' (Luke 6:21). These placed the tears as in the promise, so that they might laugh, so that they might be filled with joy.
