english: They seem to say this: 'We have been sown among the nations, we have been dispersed in many places.' But they seem to have suffered this in Babylon and Assyria alone. Therefore, what he says is this: the sowing of these seeds, such as wheat or barley, is first useful in a Gospel-like way if they are sown in the earth; for this earth receives them into its own substance through a change and transformation. For from the earth, having changed, many came from one grain; they changed from the earth into harvests. It is animated... [gap]... into the adjacent earth, and it notifies it and transforms it into its own nature.

And he says 'seeds' regarding those saying these things, the saints, saying: 'In you we shall be praised and in your name we shall confess for ever' (Ps 111:3, 9). Behold, those saying: 'With you we horn our enemies' and the others, let them say: 'You have sown us among the nations' by way of seeds, so that the nations, in a certain way, if we are sown among them in a foreign land, we might change into ourselves, and one of us might become an ear of corn bearing many grains, benefiting many souls. And those being benefited are said to be different: sometimes children of those benefiting, when those are named fathers, sometimes sheep, when those have the state and conduct of a shepherd. These therefore, as seeds having been cast down, took into themselves those being benefited from being placed before them. Having been placed, the seeds changed the earth. The nations therefore are the earth, but the seeds are those cast down for the benefit of others. Let this also be simpler: that the Assyrians have become in Babylon, though they are not many nations and all the nations are. And let this also be toward my history.

13 You sent away your people without honor (Ps 79:2). Without honor... [gap]... sent away; for having been led into captivity, we were not led there with honor, but having been led by the law of captivity; for nothing is more dishonorable than this. 'Without honor' therefore [is] 'you sent away your people'. [gap]... the people whom they wished to hold. And it is possible also to call that people, for whom... [gap]... among the others. And since 'you sent away your people without honor', that is, not having received honor, 'you sent away', [gap]... them; for they were given over to their own sins. And it is possible also that 'without honor'...

And for this reason we have endured these things, to come into captivity and to be scattered among the nations, so that you might gather to yourself. He has done to himself through sin and has made himself a debtor.

Furthermore, the thing by which the enemy, the king of souls, holds [us], is called a handwriting. And a handwriting is something which someone has fastened with his own hands. Therefore 'he took it out from the middle,' so that it might no longer hold us by the handwriting with which we had fastened ourselves, having written ourselves down in it. And are they also being written down together with themselves? —that is, us being your people, you sent away without honor (Ps 79:9)—then we were honored—by the manner of the captivity; or they speak concerning the people, for whom they themselves went into captivity: 'You sent away your people without honor' (Ps 79:9). And for this reason we endure these things, because for the sake of their help you made the same things for them to draw from again, unpleasantly.

And there was not a multitude in our substitutions. Often, for the sake of certain things, safe and redeeming substitutions are given. For instance, it says: 'It is holy everything that opens a male womb.' And it says that, if it is a firstborn sheep or an ox or a goat, among those brought to the altar, it is necessary to perform the sacrifice itself. english: Having been taken captive together... themselves and the people, and those others through sin, but the people through their own [sins] and the others through the [sins] of others. 'And there was not a multitude in their leaps' (Jonah 3:4). But few had become sufficient for... it would have happened, if they had turned back and known what evils they are in. 'Their sins are very great; I will go down and see if they have worked according to their cry coming toward me, but if not, so that I may know' (Jonah 4:2). How much [it reached] upon the cry of their wickedness and the... but if I do not find them such, but having repented like the Ninevites, I will know them. For those known by God are not trivial; 'the Lord knew those who were His' (1 Sam 2:30). 'But then, not knowing God, you served gods which are not gods by nature; but now, having known God, rather having been known by God' (Acts 17:29). When they were knowing, they were rather being known by the Benefactor.

14 A reproach has become to us from our neighbors. Regarding the history, the neighbors are the nearby ones... since therefore we were carried off into captivity, 'a reproach we have become to our neighbors' (Ps 147:2). They themselves have not suffered nor have they prevailed with the rising of wars, but we. And as for the thought of this: just as the cross of the Savior has become a reproach for the sake of salvation—for it has been said: 'counting the reproach of Christ a greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt' (Ex 12:33)—so also these have in a way fallen into reproaches, having been seized and having been led into captivity. 'Angels,' he says, 'who did not keep their own beginning, but having left their own habitation, fell into everlasting chains' (Heb 2:16). This reproach of the angels is not praiseworthy, because having been granted to dwell in heaven and being able to stand and remain beside God always praising, they became in wickedness so as to fall from heaven. This reproach is trivial. Behold, indeed, the [reproach] of Christ is not only praiseworthy, but is greater than treasures. And if there were no difference between these, the proverbist would not have said: 'Do not acquire the reproach of evil men' (Prov 22:1). When therefore the apostles [were] rejoicing...

They rejoice even while being reproached for Christ. Having done nothing [wrong], these reproaches of such people are not good. By becoming reproach itself, someone has established the practice of reproaching based on false accusations, not on truths. Thus also is the saying, 'We are without honor; for I think God has shown us the apostles to be the very last, as if marked for death' (1 Cor 4:9). This is the reproach in which they are placed. It is not a true reproach, nor is it from evil men, but from good men. Regarding the spoken word: that it is not earnest, nor God-fearing, and that those coming are our enemies, yet they did not drive us from their land.

14 They mock and deride us in our circle. The ones saying they have come not for their own sake, but for the sake of others, are holy. And they say: having been born, having held us and having drawn us into their land, being in our circle, they reproach us, mock us, and sneer at us; but the reproach, the mockery, and the derision do not touch us, but them. Just as if someone derides [another], so that they may have children by weaving themselves together, and enjoy [themselves]. Therefore, those who are being mocked by these are thought to be [such].

15 He made us a parable among the nations. Something hidden by a word is compared to something similar. That it may become clear, let us see from the Gospel (Matt 13:31): he compares the kingdom of heaven to a mustard seed, not saying 'it is like a mustard seed' while being a seed itself; for it was no longer a similarity, but an identity. He says 'hyper' [beyond/exceeding]. Therefore, the mustard seed has a power smaller in size than the seeds, capable of transforming and becoming such a plant. And the kingdom of heaven, thus revealing the teaching of the Scriptures, is something humble and small in its wording. english: The Greek word is an evangelical word. For this reason, therefore, this parable was spoken: 'for a parable' thus 'us as a nation among the nations'. If anyone wishes to interpret the captives, they use us, saying: 'Behold, these ones having been led away well before... God, when the right hand of God and the light of his face were protecting them, they fell into a most evil leading away' (Ps 78:49). If anyone therefore wishes to show a falling away, they refer to us. And 'made us a parable' is not in [Israel], not in Israel, not in the Hebrew multitude, but 'among the nations'.

Those who are truly nations do not know the difference between good and evil, but they consider all pleasant things and all appropriate things to be good, and the opposites of these to be evil. And the name of the parable may be this: the rank of the saints has a certain superiority compared to the other ranks of men. Because of this, they have become a parable. See: men are often taken captive in different ways by enemies. One suffers the taking away of what he has possessed, while another has them remaining... in the winter and the storm of this life, they have their own... flows away into corruption. 15 A head-movement among the peoples. ... they observe [those] changing from prosperity into adversity, to move... those or perhaps grieving. 224 But a head-movement among the peoples we have become. 'Peoples' indeed all the coarsest men can be called, having nothing opened, not being afraid. These therefore, because of us, set a head-movement. We, having become toward the peoples, the coarsest men, moved their mind and their head. And the mind moves when... when it perceives the things being imposed upon it to be perceived. 16 All the day my trouble is against me.

It is. He says 'all the day' and 'through life'. A man's life is called that which is from birth until death, sometimes called one day, sometimes an age. Thus it is said: 'I will not eat meat for ever' (Gen 9:4), and: 'he shall be thy servant for ever' (Ps 18:25). I had trouble against me all this day which I endured for the sake of others (Ps 34:5); and the shame of my face covered me. The shame of the inner man covered me. For my face was not destroyed, but it was covered. And it is possible, having cast off the single covering, to bear his face naked, illuminated, as it is according to nature. And, so that I may phrase it this way, the ignorance that happens to other men destroys their face; for others become from others, from men serpents and wolves and foxes. But the holy man, even if he does not bear his own face naked, has it covered. And it is covered by the arrangement of the body, becoming a seeming ignorance from the incarnation. But when a change occurs into quality, I do not say that the fox, like Herod, had a covering, but his nature and disposition were such. When someone becomes foolish among the thoughtless, having cast folly upon himself, he has his face covered; when he becomes lawless among the lawless, he has his face covered.

From a voice reproaching and speaking idly. He says this: those are reproaching me and speaking idly. And those speaking idly are straying. So he says this: those who oppose us... as the rational [being] is accustomed to have, but rather they are straying. To speak idly is to say superfluous things. From the face of an enemy and one driving [me] away. When... I endured all these things. When the enemy appeared and was pursuing... shame of the...

english: To have the face covered. I do not have these things because of wickedness... [text gapped]... immediately indeed he brought [them]: 'all these things came upon us, and we did not remember you' (Psalm 78:22). [text gapped]... because not coming out in our own powers, it came upon us to turn backward toward our enemies; it came upon us that a reproach should be placed upon our neighbors and those around us, a mockery and to have the face turned down, to be covered in shame.

Because the voice is of holy ones. Many many times also from the pleasant things they forget God, not only from the unpleasant ones. For he says: 'take care of yourself lest, having eaten and being filled and having built fine houses... the Lord your God you forget' (Deut 8:12). Sometimes, having come into afflictions, it is said they forget God. All these things came upon us, and we did not remember you, and we did not act wickedly against your covenant.

Israel was captured from Judea both by chance and locally, and a chance and natural local displacement has happened; for they thought [text gapped] having [gone] there they did not keep [the laws] there and toward the laws there [text gapped] to Babylonize according to the soul. Often God hindered them, persisting in living thus. In order that they might know by trial that evil is that which they loved, he resettled them into Babylon. Along with this, he made a way to be captured, and holy ones like Ezekiel, Zechariah, Angel, Daniel, and those cast into the furnace, so that even being there they were not completely abandoned, so that they might experience [it] as if in war.

There is also a Jerusalem above. Those living according to the divine laws dwell in God. If they become apostates from the divine laws, they are resettled into the place concerning the earth, and this is the captivity according to allegory. And there are sent out to them again here for the sake of help: 'there came a man, sent from God, his name John. This came for a testimony, so that he might testify about the light' (John 1:6-7); for he did not come for the sake of another than to testify.

To the light. Again Jeremiah hears: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb I sanctified you, and I appointed you a prophet to the nations' (Jeremiah 1:5). Before coming forth from the womb he was sanctified, and as a prophet to the nations he was appointed. Again: 'Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world' (Ephesians 1:4). By 'foundation of the world' he means his coming-to-be. And Paul and those with him were chosen before the foundation of the world, and this election has become theirs from then until now, so that they might be sent out together with those who have been called and might be able to help them.

But did Paul speak according to foreknowledge? Foreknowledge is a theoretical viewing of what is coming to be. But according to kind, foreknowledge and knowledge are the same. They differ in time. For example, suppose I foreknow that tomorrow there will be thunder. When the thunder comes to be in the middle of the day, it is knowledge, no longer foreknowledge. And the knowledge of the thunder does not make it such, but what it is, that becomes the knowledge. Thus the known thing makes the knowledge, which does not receive the knowing from us. I use an image for the sake of the manner of foreknowledge: the one [child] is born so that he may demand, and the other, so that he may live in the house. What kind of justice is this of foreknowledge, if we take these things to happen according to foreknowledge? Foreknowledge both justifies and condemns. To foreknow and to know is also to condemn and to justify from the things being done and being thought.

Paul was foreknown in this life, both a traitor and a persecutor of Christ and an apostle. Was he not both foreknown? Foreknowledge therefore made him have both. Again, did he not become first an apostle and later a traitor? He was not foreknown by God. The foreknowledge of God made him at one time an apostle and at another time a traitor. And indeed it is sought: did he choose the apostles from among us? 'Did I not choose you, the twelve?' (John 15:16) and: 'Whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son' (Romans 8:29). He does not speak about existence, but about being conformed. Foreknowledge does not lead to existence. God has made [it so], having made [them] known; for the matter does not make the knowledge of God; for the knowledge of God is eternal. source_text: πάντα πρὶν γενέσεως αὐτῶν". οὐχ ἡ πρόγνωσις δὲ ποιεῖ αὐ τὰ τοιάδε ἢ τοιάδε, ἀλλ' ἡ προαίρεσις, τὰ προαιρετικά. λέγω· προγιγνώσκω, ὅτι ὅσδε ἀρρενοτοκήσει καὶ υἱοὺς ἕξει· οὔκ ἐστιν προαιρετικὸν τοῦτο. τὸ μέντοι φαῦλον ἢ σπουδαῖον γενέσθαι ἢ ἄλλο τι ἐπιτήδευμα ἔχειν, προαιρετέα. οὐκ ἐκ προγνώσεως γίνεται, ἐπεὶ προκατακρίνει θεὸς καὶ προδικαιοῖ. εἰ δὲ προδικαιοῖ, τη῀̣ς ἀγ̣αθότητος αὐτοῦ ἦν τοῦτο τὸ πάντας δικαιῶσαι. πάλιν περὶ τοῦ Ἰσαῦ καὶ τοῦ Ἰακὼβ ὁ ἀπόστολος οἷον ἀπο̣ρήσας λέγει· "τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν πρὸς ταῦτα; μὴ ἀδικία παρὰ τῷ θεῷ; μὴ γένοιτο". διὰ τοῦ ἀνῃρηκέναι τὴν ἀδικίαν ἐβίασε̣ν η῾̣μᾶς ζητεῖν, πῶς οὐκ ἔστιν ἀδικία παρὰ τῷ θεῷ. εἰ δὲ οὕτως, ὡς οἱ λέγοντες τὴν̣ πρόγνωσιν, ἀδικίαν μᾶλλον παρ' αὐτῷ εὑρίσκομεν. "τὸν Ἰακώβ", φησίν, "ἠγάπησα καὶ τὸν Ἰσαῦ ἐμίσησα". ἐπὶ πραττομένοις δὲ μισεῖταί τις ἢ ἀγαπᾶται καὶ ἐπὶ φρονουμένοις. πῶς οὖν χώραν ἔχει ἡ πρόγνωσις; ἀδικία παρὰ τῷ θεῷ εὑρίσκεται; ἀλλὰ τοῦτο ἀναιρῶν εἶπεν· "τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; μὴ ἀδικία παρὰ τῷ θεῷ; μὴ γένοιτο". μὴ οὔσης ἀδικίας ἄλλως ζη̣τείτω τὸ πρᾶγμα, πῶς γέγονεν. πολλάκις καὶ αὐτὰ εἰρήκαμεν ὅτι· ἐὰν ὑπόλημψιν ὀρθὴν ἔχωμεν̣ περί τινος, καταλλήλως αὐτῷ 226 πάντα διανοούμεθα· ὡς ἔλεγον περὶ τοῦ βασιλέως. κατὰ πάντας δὲ τοὺς τρόπους τῆς αἰχμαλωσίας τοῦτο ἔλεγον· ἐν ἀηδέσιν πολλοῖς ·ε̣·ν̣α·ε̣ν̣η καὶ σοφοὶ ὄντες ἐν α᾿̣μφοτέροις ἡδέσιν καὶ ἀηδέσιν, καὶ οὐκ ἐγίνετο αὐτῶν λήθη θεοῦ ἐκ τούτου̣, ἀλλ' οὖν γε ἐλυποῦντο, ὅτι ἐ´̣νεισιν ἄνθρωποι τοιούτων δεόμενοι, οἷον περὶ τῶν αἰχμαλώτων, ὅτι δέονται αἰχμαλωσίας. οὕτω γοῦν ἀποδεδώκασίν τινες τὸ ἐν ἑκατοστῷ ὀγδόῳ καὶ δεκάτῳ ψαλμῷ οὕτως ἔχον· "ἀθυμία κατέσχεν με ἀπὸ ἁμαρτωλῶν". ἀθυμεῖ ὅταν ἴδῃ ἀνθρώπους λογικοὺς κατ' εἰκόνα θεοῦ καὶ καθ' ὁμοίωσιν γε̣γ̣ε̣νη̣μένους ἁμαρτάνοντας. καὶ ω῾̣ς εἴ τις πατήρ, ὅταν ἴδ̣ῃ̣ τὸν υἱὸν ἑαυτοῦ ἀπὸ πυρετοῦ καὶ παρακοπῆς τύπτοντα αὐτόν, λυπεῖται, οὐχ ὅτι τύπτει αὐτόν, ἀλλ' ὅτι εἰς τοιαύτην ἐλήλυθεν κατάστασιν, οὕτω καὶ οὗτοι γενναῖοι ὄντες καὶ εἰδότες ὅτι "διὰ πολλῶν θλίψεων εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ ἔστιν εἰσελθεῖν", οὐ πάνυ τι ἐπὶ τοῖς θλιβηροῖς καταδ̣ύονται. λέγουσιν γοῦν· "ἐν παντὶ θλιβόμεθα, ἀλλ' οὐ στενοχωρούμεθα". τὸ δὲ μὴ στενοχω̣ρεῖσθαί ἐστιν τὸ γε̣νναίως φέρειν τὰ θλιβηρά. "καὶ οὐκ ἠδικήσαμεν ἐν διαθήκῃ σου". εἰς αἰῶνα κατὰ τὸ βούλημά σου τὰ προσταχθέντα διαμένει 323 καὶ κατὰ τὰ κρίματα τὰ σά, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο οὐκ ἠδικήσαμεν. ἐὰν δέ τις λέγῃ ὅτι· "3διὰ τί ὅσδε πολύπαις̣ ἐστὶν καὶ ὅσδε ἄπαις καὶ ὅσδε πλουτεῖ καὶ ὅσδε πένεται"3; ἀδικεῖ εἰς τὴν διαθήκην τοῦ θεοῦ. ὥσπ̣ερ ἐπὶ τῶν διαθηκῶν τούτων ὧν διατίθενται ἄνθρωποι, ἐάν τις θέλῃ τινὶ τῶν ἐνγεγραμμένων ἀντιλέγειν καὶ μάχεσθαι, ματαίως ἀδικεῖ τὴν διαθήκην. ἡ αὐτοῦ ἀδικία δοκεῖ τῆς διαθήκης ἀδικία εἶναι. ἐάν τις τὴν θεόπνευστον ἑτέρως μεταχειρίζηται, ὡς οἱ ἑτερόδοξοι, ἀδικοῦσιν εἰς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, εἰς τὴν θείαν γραφήν. 19 καὶ οὐκ ἀπέστη εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω ἡ καρδία ἡμῶν. θεωρεῖς ὅτι ἐνμενόντ̣ων ἐστὶν τῇ κατ' εὐθύτητα ἀκολουθίᾳ. "οὐκ ἀπέστη εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω", οὐκ ἄλλοι γεγόναμεν ἔχοντες τὴν καρδίαν ὀρθὴν καὶ εὐθεῖαν καὶ κατ' εὐθὺ βλέπουσαν. συνβαίνει δὲ ἐφ' ἡμῶν τῶν ἀνερματίστων καὶ ἀβεβαίων τοῦτο· πολλοὶ εἰς θλῖψιν ἐληλυθότες ἀπέστρεψαν ἑαυτῶν τὴν νόησιν ὥστε γονγύζειν κατὰ τῆς προνοίας. 19 καὶ ἐξέκλινας τὰς τρίβους ἡμῶν ἀπὸ τῆς ὁδοῦ σου. τοῦτο λέγει ὅτι· καλῶς ἐτρέχαμεν τὴν ὁδόν σου πρὶν εἰς ταύτην κατήλθομεν τὴν κατάστασιν καὶ διαγωγήν. "κέκλικας τὰς τρίβους ἡμῶν ἀπὸ τῆς ὁδοῦ σου", ὅτι μετέστησας ἡμᾶς εἰς ἑτέραν ζωὴν καὶ κατάλληλον τῇ ζωῇ ὁδόν. ὅμως εἰ καὶ "ἐξέκλινας τὰς ὁδοὺς ἡμῶν" παραδοὺς ἡμᾶς εἰς αἰχμ̣αλωσίαν, ἀλλ' οὖν γε αἱ τρίβοι ἡμῶν οὐκ ἐξέκλιναν ἀπὸ τῆς ὁδοῦ σου. 20 ὅτι ἐταπείνωσας ἡμᾶς ἐν τόπῳ κακώσεως. κατ' ἀμφοτέρας τὰς ἀποδόσεις τοῦ μετοικισμοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰερουσαλὴμ εἰς τὴν Βαβυλῶνα λάβε τὸν τῆς ταπεινώσεως τόπον. κυρίω̣ς οὗτος ὁ τόπος ἐστὶν ὁ περὶ γῆν, ἔνθα ταπεινοῦνται αἱ ψυχαὶ αἱ ἐπαχ̣θιζόμεναι "τὸ σῶμα τῆς ταπεινώσεως". δύναται δὲ καὶ ὁ θλιβηροῖς παραδοθεὶς φέρειν τὴν̣ αἰσχύν̣ην καὶ κακώσεως τόπον ὅτ̣ι τὴν Ἀσσυρίαν γῆν ἢ τὴν Βαβυλωνίαν. 20 καὶ ἐπεκάλυψεν ἡμᾶς σκιὰ θανάτου. εἰ καὶ ἐπέκειτο ἐφ' ἡμῖν ὁ τῆς κακώσεως θάνατος, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐξέτριψεν ἡμᾶς. ε᾿̣π̣ε̣κάλυψεν ἡμᾶς ἡ σκιὰ αὐτοῦ. οἷον ἔστω λίθος βαρὺς ἀπαιωρημένος ἐν ὕψει. ὑπὸ τοῦτόν τις γεγονέτω, οὐ μὴν πεπτωκέτω ἐπ' αὐτόν. καὶ ὁράτω ἐνίοτε τὴν σκιὰν τοῦ
english: All before their being. It is not foreknowledge that makes things such or such, but choice, the things chosen. I say: I foreknow that this person will give birth to a male and will have sons; this is not a matter of choice. But to become something trivial or important, or to have some other fitness, is a matter of choice. It does not come from foreknowledge, since God judges beforehand and justifies beforehand. And if He justifies beforehand, it was of His goodness to justify all.

Again, concerning Esau and Jacob, the apostle, as if speaking in a dilemma, says: 'What then shall we say to this? Is there injustice with God? May it never be!' (Romans 9:14). Because he had refuted injustice, he forced us to seek how there is not injustice with God. If it were so, as those who speak of foreknowledge say, we would rather find injustice in Him. 'I loved Jacob,' He says, 'but I hated Esau' (Romans 9:13). But one is hated or loved according to things done and according to things thought. How then does foreknowledge have room? Is injustice found with God? But he, refuting this, said: 'What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? May it never be!' Since there is no injustice, let the matter be sought in another way, how it has come to pass.

Many times we have also said that: if we have a correct assumption about someone, we understand everything about him accordingly; as we were saying concerning the king. And in all the ways of captivity, he said this in many pleasures and pains, and being wise in both pleasures and pains, it did not result in God being forgotten by them, but rather they were grieved, because they were men needing such things, just as concerning the captives, that they need captivity. Thus indeed some have demonstrated that in the one hundred and eighty-first and tenth psalm it is so: 'Despondency has taken hold of me from sinners' (Psalm 181:10). One becomes despondent when he sees men made in the image of God and in likeness having become sinners. And just as if someone is a father, when he sees his son suffering from fever and weakness, he strikes him, he is grieved, not because he strikes him, but because he has come into such a state; so also these, being noble and knowing that 'through many tribulations it is necessary to enter the kingdom of God' (Acts 14:22), they do not sink entirely into the afflicted. For they say: 'In all things we are afflicted, but not in anguish' (2 Corinthians 4:8).

Not being distressed is to bear the afflictions bravely. 'And we have not acted unjustly toward your covenant' (Ps 74:22). What has been decreed according to your will remains for ever, and all things according to your judgments, and therefore we have not acted unjustly. If anyone says, 'Why is this one a child and that one a child, and this one rich and that one poor?' he acts unjustly toward the covenant of God. Just as with these covenants which men establish, if anyone wishes to contradict and fight against one of those written, he unjustly acts against the covenant in vain. His own injustice seems to be an injustice against the covenant. If anyone handles the God-breathed [Scripture] differently, as the heretics do, they act unjustly toward the Gospel, toward the Divine Scripture.

And our heart has not turned backward (Ps 73:22). You see that there is a remaining straightness of following. 'Has not turned backward' means we have not become others, having a heart that is right and straight and looking straightly. And this thing of the unsettled and the uncertain happens to us; many, having come into affliction, turned their mind so as to grumble against providence. 'And you have turned our paths from your way' (Ps 119:176). This says that we ran your way well before we descended into this condition and conduct. 'You have turned our paths from your way,' because you have transferred us into another life and a way suitable to life. However, even if 'you have turned our paths' by handing us over to captivity, nevertheless our paths did not turn away from your way.

For you have humbled us in a place of affliction (Ps 102:19). Take the place of your humbling according to both the consequences of the deportation from Jerusalem to Babylon. Primarily this place is the earth, where the souls that are brought low are humbled, 'the body of humiliation.' It can also be handed over to the afflicted to bear the shame and the place of affliction, namely the land of Assyria or the land of Babylon. english: Upon itself. And the shadow of the stone does not do what the stone itself has done, from which even God is delivered. It has been said: 'The rising sun appeared to those in darkness and the shadow of death' (Psalm 98:2).

If we have forgotten the name of our God and if we have stretched out our hands toward a foreign god, then these things are no longer said toward God himself. Previously, it was said toward God himself: 'You turned our paths from your way; you humbled us in a place of affliction' (Psalm 65:5). Therefore, they say to others that they have become in these things through sin and lawlessness, and they say: 'If we have forgotten the name of our God and if we have stretched out our hands toward a foreign god,' that is to say, if we have worshipped a foreign god. But all those called gods according to the Scripture who are falsely named should be considered foreign gods; for it has been said: 'All the gods of the nations are demons' (Psalm 95:5).

Not toward our own belly, nor toward mammon, did we stretch out our hands, which are allegorically called our deeds. [We stretched them out] toward a foreign god and toward the enemies who seem to have prevailed. God will not fail to seek these things. They were saying, in this way of reading: 'Will God not seek these things?' (Psalm 94:8) and they were saying, in this way of reading: 'Will God not seek these things?'

He says: do not think it a small thing to forget the name of God or to stretch out hands toward a foreign god. For God also seeks these things. And you know that some, especially in persecutions, were saying this: that it is possible to do things without acting with the heart. Indeed, many died saying this, and they silenced the name of God as if forgetting Him. He says, not even this [is enough to hide] God, who is invisible, and He seeks these things. For does He not seek? The following text does not permit this way of thinking. For He himself knows the secrets of the heart.

Let him who is ignorant of the secrets of the heart seek first whether he acted thus or like that. For instance, if someone, pretending to be wise, says: 'I did not stretch out my hands toward a foreign god,' I say: 'I, who am ignorant of the secrets of the heart, am examining these things.' But God does not seek; for He knows them. And He says, therefore, what He knows as secrets:

"Because of you we die all day, we were counted as sheep for slaughter" (Ps 54:3). Because of you we die all day, we were counted as sheep for slaughter. Those dying all day for God and counted as sheep for slaughter have no doubt whether they have come to the name of God or stretched hands toward a foreign god. Therefore, one does not seek these things from a heart that is manifest. "We were counted" then "as sheep for slaughter." Everyone who wishes to slaughter us can do so. And this is possible; even if some fight us, we consider ourselves as sheep being ritualized, as being sacrificed to God for a "pleasing sacrifice" (Ps 50:5). Indeed, in the Revelation of John, "the souls of those being persecuted for the testimony of Jesus" (Rev 6:9) appeared dancing under the altar of the heavenly God, clearly as victims having come there.

"Arise; why, Lord, do you sleep? Arise and do not cast us away to the end" (Ps 44:23). It seems that God sleeps when He is long-suffering toward the wrongdoing of His own holy men and the groaning of those made according to Him. Indeed, they send up a prayer saying: "Cast the hands toward their pride to the end" (Ps 54:5), and: "May the pride of those hating you ascend to you always" (Ps 54:6). And it seems God sleeps when He is long-suffering, when He overlooks His own being afflicted. "Arise and do not cast us away to the end" (Ps 44:23). For if even we have become captives and are being afflicted in the place of ill-treatment, being human, mortal, and liable to fall, we fear being cast away to the end. Israel was cast away in Babylon, when they worshiped Bel and had made the image of Nebuchadnezzar and other things of the Babylonians; they were cast away to the end. But those around Daniel, even if they were cast away locally, they were not cast away to the end; for they remained in the same godliness. It seems they were cast away, but they were not cast away to the end, the lions being silenced and him ascending unhurt.

"ἐταπεινώθη" οὖν "ἡ ψυχὴ ἡμῶν" τῶν ταῦτα λεγόντων "εἰς τὸν χοῦν". "τὸ σῶμα τῆς ταπεινώσεως" περικείμεθα, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐταπεινώθημεν ὑπ' αὐτοῦ. ὡς ἐάν τις, φέρε, πέδας λάβῃ παρὰ τυράννου τινός, δοκεῖ τεταπεινῶσθαι, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐταπεινώθη· ἔχει γὰρ τὸ αὐτὸ α᾿̣νάστημα, ἔχει τὸ αὐτὸ γαῦρος. διὰ τοῦτο πτωχοί ἐσμεν καὶ θλιβόμεθα, ὅτι ἡ ψυχὴ ἡμῶν τὸ ἴδιον̣ ἀν̣άστημα τέως φανερὸν οὐκ ἔχει ταπεινωθεῖσα εἰς τὸν χοῦν καὶ "ἡ γαστὴρ ἡμῶν τῇ γῇ ἐκολλήθη". οὐ κατὰ ἀλήθειαν δὲ τοῦτο περὶ αὐτῶν λέγουσιν, ἀλλὰ περὶ τῶν μελῶν ἑαυτῶν, περὶ τοῦ λαοῦ ἑαυτῶν. διττῶς δὲ ἔστιν ταπεινωθῆναι τὴν γαστέρ̣α εἰς τὴν γῆν· ὅταν τις τὰ ἐπίγεια φρονῇ καὶ τὰ κάτω ζητῇ, οὐ γεννᾷ οὐράνια γεννήματα, οὐ γεννᾷ λογισμοὺς θεοσεβεῖς, ἀλλὰ ἀνθρώπινα πάντα· καὶ γίνεται μήτηρ ἡ ταῦτα λέγουσα ψυχή. "ὅτι ἐκολλήθη εἰς γῆν ἡ γαστὴρ ἡμῶν". κατὰ δὲ δεύτερον λόγον ἡ τρεφομένη τῷ ἄρτῳ τῷ οὐρανίῳ, ἡ λαμβάνουσα τὴν οὐράνιον τροφὴν γαστὴρ τῷ οὐρανῷ ἐκολλήθη. ὅσοι δὲ τὰς σάρκας του῀̣ δράκοντος ἐσθίουσιν καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν φέρονται τῷ ὄφει τροφὴν γῆν οὖσαν, κολληθεῖσαν ἔχουσιν τὴν γαστέρα τῇ γῇ. καὶ ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τῶν αἰσθητ̣ω῀̣ν λέγεται· "τὰ βρώματα τῇ κοιλίᾳ, καὶ ἡ κοιλία τοῖς βρώμασιν· ὁ δὲ θεὸς καὶ ταύτην καὶ ταῦτα καταργήσει̣", οὕτω καὶ ἡ κοιλία καὶ γαστὴρ τῆς ψυχῆς ὅταν μὴ οὐράνια τραφῇ, ὅταν μὴ συνλάβῃ ἀπὸ τοῦ θείου ἑαυτῆς νυμφίου, τῇ γῇ κεκολλημένην ἔχει τὴν γαστέρα. 27 ἀνάστα, κύριε, βοήθησον ἡμῖν καὶ λύτρωσαι ἡμᾶς ἕνεκεν τοῦ ὀνόματός σου. 326 βοηθείας δεόμεθα, μὴ τὰ θλιβηρὰ ἐπὶ πολὺ παραμένοντα βλάψῃ ἡμῶν τὴν ψυχὴν τρεπτὴν οὖσαν. καὶ εἶτα, ἵνα μὴ δόξωσιν ἰδίᾳ δικαιοσύνῃ πεποιθότες λέγειν, λέγει· "ἀνάστα, κύριε, βοήθησον ἡμῖν καὶ λύτρωσαι ἡμᾶς ἕνεκεν τοῦ ὀνόματός σου". σοῦ χρηματίζομεν. διὰ τοῦτο ἐν τούτοις τοῖς ἀνιαροῖς γεγόναμεν, ὅτι σοῦ ἐσμεν, καὶ βοηθείας ἕνεκεν ἄλλων ἔπεμψας ἡμᾶς εἰς ταύτην τὴν κακοπραγίαν. 1 Εἰς τὸ τέλος, ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλλοιωθησομένων· τοῖς υἱοῖς Κόρε εἰς σύνεσιν· ᾠδὴ ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἀγαπητοῦ. ἡ ἀλλοίωσις κίνησις καὶ μεταβολή τι´̣ς̣ ἐστιν κατὰ ποιότητα. οὐ πᾶσα κίνησις καὶ μεταβολὴ ἀλλοίωσίς ἐστιν. ἔστιν γὰρ κατὰ γένεσιν μεταβληθῆναι. λέγω γοῦν τὸ ᾠὸν γίνεσθαι ὄρνεον καὶ τὸν κόκκον τοῦ σίτου στάχ̣υν. αὕτη ἡ κίνησις καὶ ἡ μεταβολὴ κατὰ γένεσίν ἐστιν. ἔστιν δὲ ἄλλη κατὰ φθορὰν γινομένη· ὁ´̣ταν φθαρῇ τὸ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου σῶμα καὶ ἀναλυθῇ εἰς ἰχῶρας καὶ σκώληκας καὶ τὰ παραπλήσια, οὐ λέγεται ἠλλοιω῀̣σθαι, ἀλλ' ἐφθάρθαι. καὶ ἔστιν καὶ ἄλλη κίνησις καὶ μεταβολὴ κατὰ αὔξησιν, ὅταν προσθήκην τοῦ προλαβόντος ποσοῦ γίνηται· ὅταν γὰρ ἐξ ἐλάττονος εἰς μεῖζον μέγεθος ἐπειχθῶ, λέγομαι ηὐξῆσθαι, με̣μειῶσθαι δὲ ὅταν συνσταλῇ τὸ ποσὸν καὶ ἐλάττω γένηται. ἡ ἀλλοίωσις οὖν κίνησίς ἐστιν κ̣ατὰ ποιότητα, οἷον ἐκ νόσου εἰς ὑγίειαν καὶ ἐξ ὑγείας εἰς νόσον, ἐξ ἀγνοίας εἰς ἐπιστήμην καὶ ἔνπαλιν, ἐξ ἀπιστίας εἰς πίστιν. "εἰς τὸ τέλος" οὖν, "ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλλοιωθησομένων". τὰ περὶ τέλους πολλάκις διεξεληλύθαμεν, ὅτι τὸ μετὰ πάντα ἐστίν, τὸ ἔσχατον ὀρεκ̣τόν. ἐστὶν τοίνυν "εἰς τὸ τέλος, ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλλοιωθησομένων". ὅταν ἡ ἀλλοίωσις ἐπίτασιν τοσαύτ̣ην σχῇ ὥστε μηκέτι δυνατὸν εἶναι περαιτέρω αὐτὴν ἐπιταθῆναι, ἐν τῷ τέλει τῶν πραγμ̣άτ̣ων, ὅτε "ὁ θεὸς πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν" γίνεται, οὐκέτι οἷόν τε ἐπεκταθῆναι τὴν ποιότητα̣. πᾶσα ἐπιστήμη καὶ πᾶσα ἀρετὴ ποιότης ἐστίν. ἔστιν οὖν ἄρξασθαι ἀρετῆς καὶ προκόπτειν ἐν ταύτῃ, καὶ ἀεὶ δυνατόν ἐστιν προσλαμβάνειν τῇ ἤδη ὑπαρξάσῃ. ὅταν δὲ τελείως τις τὴν ἀρετὴν ἔχῃ ὡς μηδὲν
english: Because of an existing wickedness. Why then do you turn away? Will you then forget our poverty and our affliction? Because of you we are afflicted, because of you we are poor. But you do not forget these things. In which [things] one conquers, even if he is gloomy or even if he is joyless. It was said that the dust is more bodily. 'Our soul was humbled' therefore, of those saying these things, 'into the dust'. 'The body of humiliation' surrounds us, but we were not humbled by it. As if someone, for instance, receives a blow from a certain tyrant, he seems to have been humbled, but he was not humbled; for he still has the same pride, he still has the same joy. Because of this we are poor and are afflicted, because our soul, having been humbled into the dust, does not clearly possess its own resurrection, and 'our belly was stuck to the earth' (Ps 22:14).

But they do not say this about them in truth, but about their own members, about their own people. And there are two ways for the belly to have been humbled to the earth: when someone thinks of earthly things and seeks lower things, he does not produce heavenly offspring, he does not produce God-fearing thoughts, but all human things; and the soul saying these things becomes a mother, 'because our belly was stuck to the earth' (Ps 22:14). And according to a second meaning, the one being nourished by the heavenly bread, the belly receiving heavenly nourishment, was stuck to heaven. But those who eat the flesh of the dragon and carry the same food to the serpent, being earth, have the belly stuck to the earth. And just as it is said concerning the sensible [things]: 'the foods to the belly, and the belly to the foods; and God will destroy both this and these' (Lk 10:19), so also the belly and the stomach of the soul, when it is not nourished by heavenly things, when it does not receive from its divine bridegroom, has the belly stuck to the earth.
Arise, Lord, help us and redeem us for the sake of your name. We ask for help, lest the afflictions remaining for a long time might harm our soul which is turning. Ka-

And then, so that they may not boast in their own righteousness, trusting in it, he says: 'Arise, O Lord, help us and redeem us for the sake of your name' (Ps 3:7). We are enriched by you. For this reason we have come into these afflictions, because we are yours, and for the sake of help you have sent us into this hardship.

1 Toward the end, for those who are being changed; to the sons of Kore for understanding; a song for the beloved. Change is a movement and a transformation of something according to quality. Not every movement and transformation is a change. For there is a change according to becoming. I say, for instance, an egg becoming a bird and a grain of wheat a stalk. This movement and transformation is according to becoming. And there is another occurring according to corruption; when the body of a human decays and is dissolved into fluids and worms and the like, it is not said to be changed, but to have decayed. And there is also another movement and transformation according to increase, when an addition to the previous amount occurs; for when I am extended from a smaller to a greater size, I am said to have increased, but to have diminished when the amount is contracted and becomes less. Change, therefore, is a movement according to quality, such as from sickness to health and from health to sickness, from ignorance to knowledge and likewise, from unbelief to faith.

'Toward the end,' therefore, 'for those who are being changed.' We have often explained regarding the end, that it is that which is after all things, the last thing to be desired. Thus, 'toward the end, for those who are being changed.' When change reaches such a limit that it is no longer possible for it to be further extended, in the perfection of things, when 'God becomes all in all' (1 Cor 15:28), the quality can no longer be extended. Every knowledge and every virtue is a quality. It is possible, therefore, to begin virtue and to make progress in it, and it is always possible to receive [more] to that which already exists. "εἰς τὸ τέλος" οὖν, "ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλλοιωθησομένων". ταύτην δὲ τὴν μακαρίαν καὶ θείαν καὶ ὑπερφυ̣ῆ ἀλλοίωσι̣ν ἔχομεν ἐκ τῆς τοῦ ὑψίστου δεξιᾶς· εἴρηται γὰρ περὶ αὐτῆς· "αὕτη ἡ ἀλλοίωσις τῆς δεξιᾶς τοῦ ὑψίστου"· ὥσπερ γὰρ "πλούσιος ὢν δι' ἡμᾶς ἐπτώχευσεν, ἵνα τῇ αὐτοῦ πτωχείᾳ πλούσιοι γενώμεθα"–καὶ ὅρα· "πλούσιος ὢν δι' ἡμᾶς ἐπτώχευσεν"· καὶ γὰρ ἀλλοιωθεὶς καὶ ἐπιδημήσας. καὶ μένων χωρὶς τῆς ἐπιδημίας ὁ αὐτός ἐστιν, ἀεὶ ἔχει τὸ εἶναι πλούσιος. "δι' ἡμᾶς" δε`̣ ἐπ̣τώχευσεν". ὅταν τοίνυν δι' ἡμᾶς πτωχεύσας πλουσίους ἡμᾶς καταστήσῃ, ἀλλοιούμεθα κατὰ πλοῦτον καὶ εἰς τὸ τέλος ἐρχόμεθα, ἐὰν ὡς αὐτὸς γενώμεθα πλούσιοι, ὡς ἐνδέχεται, ὁ´̣τ̣αν θεασώμεθα "τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ, δόξαν ὡς μονογενοῦς παρὰ πατρός, πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας". "ἐκ τοῦ πληρώματος" οὖν λαμ̣βάνουσιν οἱ ἅγιοι. οὐδεὶς τὸ πλήρωμα δέχεται, οὐδὲ πάντες. οὕτω καὶ τό· "ἐκχεῶ ἀπὸ τοῦ πνεύματός μου". οὐκ εἶπεν· "τὸ πνεῦμά μου"· "ἀρραβῶνα" γὰρ "πνεύματος" λαμβάνο̣υ̣σιν οἱ ἐνταῦθα πνευματοφ̣όροι. καὶ ἐκχεῖται ὁ ἀρραβὼν ἀπὸ τοῦ πνεύματος. ὁ δὲ ἀρραβὼν ὅλου τινὸς μέρος ἐστίν. "εἰς τὸ τε´̣λος̣" οὖν, "ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλλοιωθησομένων". "αὕτη" οὖν "ἡ ἀλλοίωσις τῆς δεξιᾶς τοῦ ὑψίστου". ἡ δεξιὰ τοῦ ὑψ̣ι´̣ς̣του ἄτρεπτος καὶ ἀναλλοίωτός ἐστιν. ἀεὶ κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως ἔχει· οὐκ ἄλλως γὰρ αὐτὴν ἢ τὸν σωτῆρα νοοῦμεν. πῶς οὖν ἀλλοιοῦται, ἴδω̣μ̣εν· συνκαταβαίνει παιδεύουσα· καὶ τότε τῷ ὄντι ὠφελούμεθα, ἐὰν συνκαταβῇ. μενού σης δὲ αὐτῆς ἐφ' ἑαυτὴν ἡμεῖς οὐκ ὠφελούμεθα. λέγει οὖν τοῦτο· "μὴ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας ἀπώσεται κύρι328 ος ἢ ἐπιλήσεται τοῦ οἰκτιρῆσαι"; ἔτι· "ἢ ἀποκόψει τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ γενεᾶς εἰς γενεὰν ἢ συνέξει τοὺς οἰκτιρμοὺς αὐτοῦ"; λέγει· "καὶ εἶπα Νῦν ἠρξάμην", ὅτε συνκαταβαινούσης πεῖραν ἔλαβον τῆς δεξιᾶς. "νῦν ἠρξάμην"· ἐν ἀρχῇ γέγονεν τοῦ γνῶναι τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ἐν ἀρχῇ τοῦ γνῶναι τὰ ἔργα τῆς προνοίας, τοὺς οἰκτιρμο̣ὺς τοῦ θεοῦ τοὺς ποιητικοὺς ἀγαθοῦ. "εἶπα" οὖν "Νῦν ἠρξάμην". λέγει· "αὕτη ἡ ἀλλοίωσις", ἣν ὑπέμεινα ἐγώ, "τῆς δεξιᾶς τοῦ ὑψίστου" ἐστίν. αὕτη με ἠλλοίωσεν. οὐδεὶς ἠδύνατο τῶν γε̣νητῶν ἀλλοιῶσαί με οὕτως· πάντες γὰρ δέονται τοῦ εἰς προκοπὴν ἄγοντος, τοῦ τελειοῦντος. δημωδέστερον δὲ καὶ κατὰ τοὺς εἰς μέσον λέγοντας ἐροῦμεν ὅτι ἡ ἀλλοίωσις τοῦ ὑψίστου αὕτη ἐστίν· εὐλογία ὢν γέγονε κατάρα, ἵν' ἀπολύσῃ κατάρας καὶ εὐλογουμένους ἀποδείξῃ. δικαιοσύνη ὠ`̣ν γέγονεν οὖν ἁμαρτία, ἁμαρτία δὲ τοιαύτη δικαιοσύνης ποιητική. "ἐν αὐτῷ" δὲ γινόμεθα "δικ̣αιοσύνη ς ποιητική θεοῦ". οὐκ ἁπλῶς οὖν δικαιοσύνη, ἀλλὰ θεοῦ. εἰρήκαμεν πολλάκις, ὅτι τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν ἕξε̣ων 230 ἔχουσιν οἱ παρονομαζόμενοι, ὅταν τελειωθῶσιν κατ' αὐτά. οὕτω γοῦν καὶ τὸν ἐν ἀγάπῃ τελειωθέντα, ὡς ἐνδέχεται ἐν τῷ βίῳ, ἀγάπην ὀνομάζει Παῦλος· τὸ γάρ· "ἡ ἀγάπη οὐ φυσιοῦται, ου᾿̣κ ἀσχημονεῖ, οὐ περπερεύεται", οὐ περὶ τῆς ἀγάπης τῆς ἀρετῆς λέγεται, τῆς ἐντολῆς τῆς πασῶν μείζονος, ἀλλὰ περὶ τοῦ ἔχοντος, περὶ τοῦ ποιοῦ. γίνεται οὖν ὁ σωτὴρ πάντα ἡμῶν ἕνεκα. γίνεται σάρξ, "ἵν' ἡμεῖς δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ γενώμεθα"· θεασάμενοι γὰρ "τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ, δόξαν ὡς μονογενοῦς", οὐ
english: To be transformed into something else until the end. The same applies to knowledge and wisdom; we say the same thing: there is one being introduced into wisdom who is subject to testing as one capable of sinning. For it is said, 'reprove the wise, and he will love you' (Prov 9:8). No one is reproved unless he possesses the things by which he is to be reproved. This wise person, who is subject to testing, is a newborn and, being just brought in, is able to make progress continually. But when he receives wisdom such that it is no longer possible to receive it as an addition, he has been transformed until the end.

And here, even if many saints were being influenced by 'the body of humility,' they receive 'out of His fullness,' not the fullness itself, nor each one out of the fullness, but 'all from the fullness.' And they receive here 'a pledge of the Spirit,' not the whole Spirit itself, so that I may phrase it this way. But when 'the partial' is abolished and the end remains, and 'face to face' is seen, and men become like God according to what has been said: 'when He is revealed, we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is' (2 Cor 5:17), here is the end of those being transformed. And it is well to say 'those being transformed' and not 'those having been transformed.'

No one is praised for knowledge and virtue if he merely became knowledgeable or virtuous, but when he is [actively] knowledgeable; for virtue and knowledge belong to the active, having their being in the act of being. Therefore, 'unto the end,' 'on behalf of those being transformed.' This blessedness, divine and superlative transformation, we have from the right hand of the Most High; for it is said concerning it: 'this is the transformation of the right hand of the Most High.' Just as it is said, 'being rich, He became poor for our sake, so that through His poverty we might become rich' (2 Cor 8:9)—and see: 'being rich, He became poor for our sake'—for having been transformed, He also made His presence felt. But remaining apart from His presence, He is the same, always possessing being as rich. 'For our sake' He became poor. Therefore, when having become poor for our sake, He makes us rich, we are being transformed in wealth and are coming unto the end, if we become rich as He is, as is possible, whenever we behold 'His glory, the glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth' (John 1:14). Thus, the saints receive 'out of the fullness.' No one receives the fullness, nor all...

In the same way with the words, 'I will pour out from my Spirit.' He did not say, 'my spirit'; for those who are spirit-bearers here receive a 'pledge' of the 'Spirit.' And the pledge is poured out from the Spirit. And the pledge is a part of a whole. Therefore, 'unto the end,' 'concerning those who shall be transformed.'

So, 'this is the transformation of the right hand of the Most High.' The right hand of the Most High is unshakeable and unchangeable. It always has and is the same; for we understand it as nothing other than the Savior. How then is it transformed, let us see: it descends along with [us] to instruct; and then, in reality, we were benefited if it descends along with us. But if it remains above itself, we are not benefited.

Therefore he says this: 'Will the Lord cast off forever or withhold his mercy?' (Ps 89:3) and 'Will he cut off his mercy from generation to generation or withhold his compassions?' (Ps 89:3) He says: 'And I said, Now I have begun,' when, through the descending [process], I received experience of the right hand. 'Now I have begun': it happened in the beginning to know the truth, in the beginning to know the works of providence, the creative mercies of God toward good. So I said, 'Now I have begun.'

He says: 'This transformation,' which I endured, 'of the right hand of the Most High' is. This transformed me. No one of the created things was able to transform me in this way; for all need one who leads toward progress, one who perfects. But speaking more popularly and for those speaking in the middle, we will say that this is the transformation of the Most High: being a blessing, it has become a curse, so that it may release the curse and demonstrate those who are blessed. Being righteousness, it has therefore become sin, but sin such as is a maker of righteousness. And 'in him' we become 'the creative righteousness of God.' It is not righteousness simply, but of God.

We have said many times that those who are renamed possess the names of the seven [gifts] when they are perfected according to them. In the same way, regarding the one perfected in love, as is possible in life, Paul calls it love; for 'love does not boast, is not rude, does not seek its own' (1 Cor 13:4) is not said concerning the virtue of love, the commandment which is greater than all, but concerning the one possessing it, concerning the one doing it. Therefore the Savior becomes for the sake of all of us. "εἰς τὸ τέλος" οὖν, "ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλλοιωθησομε´̣νων"· οἱ ἀλλοιωθησόμενοι οὗτοι οἱ ἔτι ἐν τῷ ἀλλοιοῦσθαι ὄντες φθάσουσίν ποτε εἰς τὸ τέλος τη῀̣ς̣ ἀλλοιώσεως· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἄρχεταί τις, ἵνα μὴ τελειωθῇ, ἀλλ' ἵνα μετὰ πολλὰς προκοπὰς εἰς αὐτὸ τὸ πέρας τῆς ποιότητος ἐκείνης καθ' ἣν ἀλλοιοῦται, φθάσῃ. τί δὲ τὸ τέλος ἢ τὸ θεοποιηθῆναι, ἵνα πάντα ᾖ; τινὲς λαμβάνουσιν αὐτὸ περὶ τη῀̣ς̣ ἀναστάσεως τῆς ἐκ νεκρῶν λέγοντες τοὺς ἐγειρομέν̣ους ἀντὶ φθαρτοῦ σώματος ἄφθαρτον ἔχοντας καὶ ἀντὶ ψυχικοῦ πνευματικὸν καὶ ἀν̣τ̣ὶ ἀσθενοῦς καὶ ἀδ̣όξου ἰσχυρὸν καὶ ἔνδοξον. ψυχὴ μένει. κατὰ ἀλλοίωσιν δὲ ἡ μεταβολὴ γέγονεν. ἐὰν οὖν κατὰ ἀλλοίωσιν ἀνάστασις γένηται, ἡ σὰρξ πάλιν σάρξ ἐστιν, τὸ φθαρτὸν πάλιν φθαρτόν ἐστιν· οὐ γὰρ ποιότητα λέγω τὸ φθαρτὸν ἢ τὴν σάρκα. κατὰ ἀλλαγὴν λέγω οὐκ ἐξ ὑποκειμένου εἰς ἄλλο ὑποκείμενον, ἀλλὰ εἰς γενάμενον ἐκ φθαρέντος γεγονέναι. φθείρεται τὸ νίτρον καὶ ἡ ἄμμος καὶ γίνεται ἡ ὕελος. ἡ φθορὰ δὲ τούτων οὐκ εἰς τὸ μὴ ὂν αὐτὰ κ̣αταστρ̣έφει. καὶ τὸ τοῦ ὀστράκου, ὡς εἶπον, τὸ ἐκ πυρὸς ὄστρακον γεγενημένον οὐκ εἰς τὸ μὴ ὀ`̣ν κα̣ταβάλλει τὸν πηλόν, καὶ γίνεται τὸ ὄστρακον ἑτέρωθέν ποθεν. ὡσαύτως ἐξ ᾠοῦ γίνεται τὸ ὄρ̣νεον· μὴ english: We remain flesh, but we become gods according to those 'to whom the word of God became' (John 1:14). This 'alteration' is according to both, that is, both that which we others have been altered into and that which was undergone on our account; it is not a turning away, nor having been altered according to the divinity, but according to the economy, according to the humanization. 'Unto the end' therefore, 'for the sake of those who shall be altered'; these ones who are to be altered, while still being in the process of being altered, will one day reach the end of that alteration; for no one begins in order that he might not be perfected, but in order that after many progresses he might reach that very end of that quality according to which he is being altered.

And what is the end, or the becoming god-like, so that all might be? Some take this regarding the resurrection from the dead, saying that those being raised have an incorruptible instead of a corruptible body, and a spiritual instead of a psychic, and a strong and glorious instead of a weak and dishonorable. But Paul, saying, did not say: 'all shall be altered', but 'we shall be changed' (1 Cor 15:51), 'and the dead shall be raised incorruptible' (1 Cor 15:52), since the body is raised according to essence; for from a body an incorporeal thing does not become, but from such a body a certain kind of body becomes, having the change according to quality.

If we take it thus according to quality only, it is an alteration. But if, since the corruptible is not the same as the incorruptible, the corruptible becomes incorruptible, it is a change, a change according to transformation. I do not say that from a body an incorporeal thing has become, but from a corruptible body an incorruptible body. But does the body remain? The body remains, and just as a sinful soul, if it becomes righteous, the soul remains. But the change has happened according to alteration. If, therefore, a resurrection happens according to alteration, the flesh is flesh again, the corruptible is corruptible again; for I am not speaking of the quality of the corruptible or the flesh. It happens according to change.

If, for example, we change the colors of a vessel made from a shell either by painting or otherwise, this is altered; for the same thing remains. But if, having made a vessel from clay, we bring it to the fire and it becomes a shell, this is not an alteration, but a change, not because the clay was cast out and the shell was brought in, but because that thing has become shell-like. Again, the sand and nitre having been prepared by the glass-makers, glass is made...

It is a kind of [change], and I do not say that the sand has vanished as if it had departed, or the saltpeter, but rather those things have become natron. And listen to the fact that there is a change: when the saltpeter was saltpeter, it was dissolved upon the passing of moisture, but the natron having come from it is not dissolved. Again, the sand was seed upon the passing of moisture. But when it becomes natron, it is no longer seed. I say, therefore, that this is a change, not from one underlying substance into another underlying substance, but into something having come into being from that which has undergone corruption. The saltpeter and the sand undergo corruption and become natron. Yet the corruption of these does not destroy them into non-existence.

And the matter of the pottery, as I have said, the clay having become a pot through fire, does not cast the clay down into non-existence, but the pot becomes something else from it. Likewise, the bird comes from an egg; for the egg is not cast out from the outside so that the bird might be brought in; rather, that very thing transforms into this, yet it is no longer an egg; for it flies, and it has sensation. The egg has endured none of these things. And Paul has used the name of the seed: 'it is sown in corruption, it is sown in weakness' (1 Cor 15:43). I say: the seed of the animal, when it is a seed, is not an animal. But it transforms itself into the animal; for it is not that an animal comes from somewhere else after the seed has vanished, but the seed itself, first being turned into nature, then from nature into an embryo, and after the embryo, becoming an animal, undergoes birth. These, then, are changes, not alterations; for change does not occur by quality alone. And many such things are to be found.

And Paul himself, using the seeds: the grain of wheat is a grain before it is sown. But when it happens to be sown in agriculture, it becomes an ear; or, as others say, again wheat. But they did not know that what was said is an example. It has been said many times that examples are not made uniform, because they are no longer examples. Again, it is not the same thing to be an infant and a child. Nevertheless, the infant transforms into the child, and I do not say that the child entered from somewhere else after the infant had been turned into non-existence, but the infant itself, through growth and through another quality, became a child, without having reached maturity. source_text: μεθηλικιούμενον ἄνθρωπον οὐκ ἔνι διαφορά· εἷς γὰρ ὑποκείμενος τῷ βρέφει ἐκείνῳ καὶ τῇ ἡλικίᾳ ἐκείνῃ· ἀπολωλός, πάλιν ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν τῷ παιδὶ ὑποκείμενος. καὶ ἐὰν ἐκ τοῦ παιδὸς εἰς τὸν βούπαιδα μεταβάλῃ, πάλιν ἡ ἡλικία μετέβαλεν. ἐστὶν δὲ ποιότης αὕτη, ποιότης δ̣ὲ οὐσιώδης. καὶ πάλιν ἀεὶ μεθηλικιούμενον ἕως φθάσῃ εἰς τὸ γῆρας. ποιότητας οὖν κ̣αὶ ἡλικίας ἐξαλλάττει· εἶπον γὰρ τὰς ἡλικίας οὐσιώδεις εἶναι ποιότητας. ὁ αὐτὸς δὲ ἄνθρωπος μένει. κἂν μυρίαν οὖν μεταβολὴν δέξηται τὸ σῶμα ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει, σῶμά ἐστιν̣, οὐ σῶμα μέντοι τόδε, οὐ τὸ πρὸ τῆς μεταβολῆς. καὶ ὁ Παῦλος γοῦν ἠναγκάσθη ὡς ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο εἰπεῖν. εἶπεν δὲ ὅτι· "σπείρεται σῶμα ψυχικόν, ἐγείρεται σῶμα πνευματικόν". λέγει· "οὐ πρῶτον τὸ πνευματικὸν ἀλλὰ τὸ ψυχικόν, ἔπειτα τὸ πνευματικόν". ἔνθα δὲ τὸ πρῶτον καὶ τὸ ἔπειτα, οὐ ταὐτότης σημαίνεται. ὅμως δὲ τὸ πρῶτον καὶ τὸ ἔπειτα οὐκ ἐπὶ ἐξαλλαγῆς οὐσιῶν λαμβάνομεν, ἀλλὰ ἐξαλλαγῆς τοῦ αὐτοῦ σώματος, ἐπ̣εὶ ἐκ̣ φθαρτοῦ ἄφθαρτον καὶ ἐκ ψυχικοῦ πνευματικὸν γέγονεν. ἄλλο οὖν ἐστιν ἀλλαγὴ καὶ ἄλλο ἀλλοίωσις. ἡ μεταβολὴ τῆς ψυχη῀̣ς ποιεῖ τὴν ἀλλοίωσιν, τὴν ἐπαινουμένην λέγω ἢ καὶ τ̣ὴν ψ̣ε̣γομένην· καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ χεῖρον γὰρ̣ ἔστιν ἀλλοιω θῆναι, ὡς εἴρηται· "πῶς ἀμαυρωθήσεται τὸ χρυσίον, πῶς ἀλλοιωθήσεται τὸ ἀργύριον τὸ ἀγαθόν"; καὶ λέγει· "υἱοὶ Σιὼν οἱ τίμιοι ἐπηρμένοι χρυσίῳ καὶ ἀργυρίῳ, πῶς ἐλογίσθησαν εἰς ἀγγεῖα ὀστράκινα ἔργα χειρῶν" ἑαυτῶν; ἄλλα π̣άλιν δ̣είξει ἀλληγορία· χρυσίον γὰρ εἰς ὀστράκινα σκεύη μεταβεβληκέναι λέγεται οὐ κατ' ἱστορίαν, ἀλλὰ κατὰ ἀναγωγήν. "εἰς τὸ τέλος" οὖν, "ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλλοιωθησομένων· τοῖς υἱοῖς Κόρε εἰς σύνεσιν". καὶ ἐπεὶ αὐτὴ ἡ ἐπιγραφὴ καὶ ὅλος ὁ ψαλμὸς μυστήρια ἔχει ἐνκεκρυμμένα, διὰ τοῦτο συνέσεως χρεία τῷ τὴν ᾠδὴν ταύτην προφέροντι· "εἰς σύνεσιν" γάρ ἐστιν. καὶ ἔλεγον καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ τριακοστοῦ πρώτου ψαλμοῦ, ἐπεὶ μετ' αἰνιγμοῦ ἐλέχθη. english: There is no difference in a man who is growing older; for there is one underlying subject to that infant and that age; having perished, he is again a man underlying the child. And if he changes from the child to an ox, the age has changed again. And this is a quality, and it is a non-substantial quality. And again, always growing older until he reaches old age. Therefore, qualities and ages are being exchanged; for he said that ages are qualities that are non-substantial. But the same man remains.

Even if the body receives ten thousand changes in the resurrection, it is a body, but not this body, not the one before the change. And Paul, therefore, was compelled to speak as one thing and another. He said: 'A natural body is sown, a spiritual body is raised' (1 Cor 15:44). He says: 'Not first the spiritual but the natural, then the spiritual.' And where there is the first and the second, identity is not signified. However, we do not take the first and the second as an exchange of substances, but an exchange of the same body, since it has become incorruptible from the corruptible and spiritual from the natural. So one thing is change and another is alteration. The change of the soul effects the alteration, which I call the praised or even the lied-about; for it is easier to undergo alteration, as it has been said: 'How shall the gold be darkened? How shall the good silver be altered?' (Ps 119:127). And he says: 'Children of Zion, the precious ones, overlaid with gold and silver, how were they counted as vessels of earthenware, the work of their own hands?' (Ps 12:6).

Again, allegory will show other things; for it is said that gold has been changed into earthenware vessels, not according to history, but according to anagogical ascent. 'Unto the end,' therefore, 'for those who shall be altered; to the sons of Kore for understanding.' And since the inscription itself and the whole psalm have mysteries hidden within them, for this reason understanding is needed for the one bringing this song; for it is 'for understanding.' And it was also said concerning the three hundred and first psalm, since it was spoken with an enigma: 'A song, therefore, for the beloved.' This very triumphal song became for the beloved; for he himself became the cause of the alteration; for he said that 'being rich, he became poor,' so that he might work us to be rich, not rich according to a fantasy, not sensually, but having...

"Every word and all knowledge." He said that having become cursed, he established a blessing. Therefore, the beloved has become the cause of this best of transformations. For this reason, the song is assigned to him; just as a victory song is sent to a general or a king, even though others, spear-bearers and soldiers, are accompanying him, yet the essence of the victory is inscribed to the king or the general.

What about "for the sake of the beloved"? Instead of "concerning"—for it is not always said "on behalf of something"; "so that the one against [him] may be entangled, having nothing to say something trivial concerning us"; for it is not said here "concerning us" instead of "gathering for us."

"My heart searched out a good word" (Psalm 63:3). Some take this psalm to be spoken from the presence of the Father and from the presence of the perfect man, the wise one. And you know that the eructation of previously eaten food brings forth its fragrance; for there is no eructation other than a proceeding of spirit from the stomach declaring the quality of the things previously eaten. If indeed anyone eats an apple, he has the eructation bringing forth the quality and fragrance of the apple.

When therefore a holy person eats the "bread of life" (John 6:35) and having Jesus' flesh as true food and the fruits of the "tree of life" (Genesis 2:9) and drinks the wine being harvested from the "true vine" (John 15:1), he has an eructation suitable to the foods previously eaten. He who has thus been fed and has eructated signifies: "the good man out of the good treasure of the heart brings forth the good" (Luke 6:45). And since it is concerning spiritual things, he was not hesitant to speak of a treasure instead of stomachs, namely the heart.

He who therefore has been fed on the blessed food and has enjoyed the flesh of Jesus and the "bread of life" (John 6:35), the bread of heaven, brings forth words suitable to that which he was fed and eructated: "my heart searched out a good word" (Psalm 63:3). We have therefore spoken fully concerning the man.

The sons of Korah, bringing the hymns with this same mind and the same spirit, bring them forth as one. Just as: "as the deer longs for the water springs, so my soul longs" (Psalm 42:1), so also here they say as one and in unison: "my heart searched out." And this refers to each of the wise; for if the wise man [brings forth] what he has in his heart and what he was fed, these [things]...

πλήρωμα οὖν τῶν καλῶν, τὸ πλη´̣ρωμα τυγχάνων τῶν ἀρετω῀̣ν λέγεται πηγή. καὶ ἡ ἐκ πατρὸς τοίνυν τοῦ 233 σωτῆρος γέννησις οὐ πρόχειρος οὖσα οὐδὲ λημπτὴ τοῖς θέλουσιν, ἀλλ' ἐκείνοις μόνοις, οἷς english: He brings it forth by instructing, having searched out the good word. From this, the word again gathers this point: that if anyone wishes to bring forth a word without having been nourished, it is not a good movement. And again, just as a handler, having nourished himself on food, has a reason for instruction, so he says, 'I declare my works to the king.' My works are so boldly declared, and they bring me no condemnation nor any reproach. I say to him, to the king, to the judge.

My tongue is a scribe's pen, sharp-writing. My word is signified through the tongue. Often you will find the tongue used instead of the word. As if he says, 'The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the great-sounding tongue' (Psalm 12:2), he calls the word 'great-sounding'. It is a beautiful beauty according to the sons of men. And the sons of men—that is, the wise of the world and those who once promised teaching—seem to have beauty in their own words. Our word's beauty according to the sons of men is sent by God, is a gift from God, and is true wisdom. Therefore, it possesses something more than the sons of men who, speaking from their own hearts, gather words and lessons of their own zeal and learning.

For then listen: the Psalm is received from the face of the Father. And almost all those speaking to the common people receive it in this way. The transcendent and great things, which are above the intellects, are revealed only through many examples. Wishing therefore to say many times that God is one, we say ten thousand things. We say that nothing is joined to Him, that there is neither matter nor form in Him, that He is a Monad, He is a One, and only through a multitude of words do we make these things manifest. But when I wish to speak about wine, it is enough to say 'wine'; for they know what it is, it is said; and we signify only the concept through the word. The same is true concerning earth. We have no need of many words. But when we say that the...
God is land, saying: 'Did I become a desert to Israel or a tilled land?' (Isa 54:3). We say ten thousand things to show how God is called land.

Again, if we call him a source, we do not say little, as when we report concerning a sensible source. But concerning God we say many things, because since the things pertaining to God and the fullness of his goodness are not externally being thrust upon or supplied, but he himself is full of goodness. Therefore, the fullness of the good things, the fullness of those happening to be virtuous, is called a source.

And the generation of the Savior from the Father is not something readily available nor to be taken by those wishing, but only to those to whom a revelation of the Father and of the Son has become; for just as the Father reveals the Son and the Son the Father, many examples are needed so that the intimacy of the Son toward the Father and the generation may be made manifest. For he calls him 'the radiance of light.' The radiance is not external to the light; it is generated from it. And the light does not pre-exist the radiance; for light and radiance are simultaneous. If, therefore, we wish to show that it is an eternal generation of the Son, we call him an eternal radiance of light from the eternal.

But the heterodox do not know how each of these things is said, and they do not take them as models, but say: 'The light is essence, the radiance is energy. Is the Son not energy of essence and not essence?' They do not understand why this was said: so that one might learn that the Father does not pre-exist the Son; for the Father is not a sensible light and the Son is not a sensible radiance. It has become a teaching upon human things, so that from those things which we know, we may learn what we do not know. But we know that the light does not pre-exist the radiance.

Again, the Father is called a source of wisdom; for 'you have left' the 'source of wisdom' (Jer 2:13). He wishes to show that just as the water of the source is not foreign, so also the wisdom of the 'only wise one' is not [foreign].

english: For he says 'only wise' of the Father, not having said 'only wise' of any of the created things; for many are those called by a name from which they possess wisdom. But the Father is not called wise by a name from wisdom, since he was no longer alone, there being many participating in wisdom and being called wise from it, but he is called 'only wise' because he springs forth wisdom, begetting wisdom, so that the 'only wise' could not say wisdom and call the wisdom 'only wise', as it is to be wise from the wise.

And here, therefore, again, the Word, desiring to show the essential relationship of the Son to the Father and the generation from him, calls the Father the source of wisdom and the source of life; for he is also called the source of life: 'You abandoned me, the spring of living water' (Jeremiah 2:13). And here, therefore, again, the Word, desiring to show that the Savior is not of another essence than the Father's, says that he himself has drawn a word from the heart: 'for my heart has drawn out a good word' (Psalm 62:8). For God has a heart, and no other heart of his own; for the heart signifies the mind. And he is that very mind. And just as it is said that he has immortality not from another beside him and has life in himself not being another existing of his, so also he has a heart not being another of his; for he is mind, and the Son is the offspring of mind. And the Word is the offspring of mind. Therefore, 'my heart has drawn out a good word'.

And in order that he might show that it is not the heart that begot, and that the offspring is good, he said the offspring; for it is indubitable that if the offspring is good, it is not the case that the begetter must be good. But perhaps it is not always saved. It happens that something begotten from the good is not good when it undergoes a change. But since the Word is unchangeable and does not have as the others a changeable state, so also the good received its generation from the heart of the good Father. Again, since among humans the things brought forth from the womb are genuine offspring, he says again: 'I begot you from the womb before the Morning Star' (Luke 1:31). To beget is a property of the womb, just as to do is a property of the hands. When, therefore, he wishes to introduce God as a genuine maker and truly the creator of creation, he says the works of his hands are the creation: 'I will see the heavens, the works of your fingers' (Psalm 8:3). 'The heavens are the works of my hands'. And since some think that the...

To beget and to create are the same; thus, if one were to say, 'the heavens are the products of my hands,' or to say, 'I begot you from a hand,' it is not that they are different, but that they differ according to thought. Yet the indwelling is manifest through all these from the Father. As I said a little earlier, if someone names one thing only sensually, they name it by the name of the Lord. I say all these things regarding God, so that through all things I may remain apart from those capable of speaking falsely concerning God.

And here, then, the heart of the Father begets. And regarding human beings, I say this—at times they become begetters of thoughts, at other times they receive them from without through instruction. Therefore, they are not called fathers of thoughts if they have been made such by something else alone. For we certainly call the discoverers of the sciences 'fathers of the sciences,' but we do not call those who have learned from others 'fathers of the sciences.'

For they say, for instance, that Moses first became a father of legislation because he did not receive the laws from another, but was himself called by God to this end. 'My heart drew out a good word' (Psalm 40:8). Just as an offspring comes from the womb, so also the good word is in the heart. And a heart toward God and a womb are not one thing and another. 'I declare my works to the king.' A change of person has occurred here.

The good word himself, being begotten and in agreement with the Father, says, 'I declare my works to the king'; for just as when we hear, 'God said, Let there be' (Genesis 1:3), and, 'He said, and they came into being; He commanded, and they were created,' we do not hear these things in a human way; for He is not ignorant of the Son what must come to be and how; He commanded and said, but because of us, so that the agreement of the Father and the Son might be shown, that all things came to be by a single will and all things are provided for. For, 'God said, Let there be' (Genesis 1:3), do you think He used a spoken word? We say that the work reaches the word, and the word is not prior in time to the work, but is in thought alone. If then this is the case, how must it be said that we hear? We do not hear by a passing voice, from a mouth passing into the hearing of the voice. english: Concerning the Spirit, of whom the Savior said, 'He cannot speak of himself' (John 16:13). This 'cannot' means that apart from Him and the Father, His word or teaching is not brought forth. Regarding others, it signifies that many are generated [erroneously], because someone speaks apart from God when he does this wrongly.

But the Holy Spirit does not possess the nature of being separated from the Father's announcement; to phrase it thus, He is the announcement itself. For I say, 'I declare my works to the King.' The Savior says, 'My tongue is a sharp scribe's pen.' My tongue writes incorruptible laws in the hearts of men; for He is 'giving laws upon their mind, and upon their heart I will write them' (Hebrews 8:10). And God writes through His living Spirit upon the fleshly hearts, and not the stony ones. And behold, the sharp scribe's pen is able to be the Holy Spirit. He writes sharply... they are [through] understanding: 'Once God spoke, twice these things I have heard' (Job 33:14). And in the word of the one set forth... is [water/refreshment].

And I have said twice: 'Once God spoke, twice these things I have heard.' And... that... if it is being demonstrated concerning circumcision, the wise man hears two: one concerning the sensory [circumcision] according to the commandment, and one concerning the spiritual. If they spoke once of God concerning sacrifice, again we hear these two: the sensory circumcision according to the law, and that carried up by the Spirit, called the 'sacrifice of praise.' And for each commandment it is the same: concerning the Sabbath, if he says, 'twice these things he heard.'

But they were saying another, higher understanding, which is harsh to the many, that: God, desiring to command His many [laws], such as the Decalogue, does not speak according to one single commandment, but... having come into the listener's mind, all was heard. 'Twice these things I heard,' so that you might receive more than just these. It is so; and indeed it is clear to the many; nevertheless let us see: the thought and the spoken word are not the same. Thought is the activity of the mind, of which the voice is a symbol. 'Those in the soul's sufferings are a symbol of those in the voice.' But the spoken word is that...

english: God wills it, just as one made to guard and work beside him. Similarly, we do not set aside this thing by saying something outside the word, as if when I converse, announce, or think, we do not set aside all things of the soul nor all things of the body, but he who sits together from both sides says what he thinks. And this activity is of the soul, as the composer says. If I say that I walk slowly or grow warm or shiver, the composer is now concerning his own body.

'My tongue is like a scribe's sharp pen. He beautifies with grace among the sons of men' (Isa 50:4). The evangelical word is among all these human words. Of the man who received and anticipated the word of God, the word is good and kingly. Grace was poured out on your lips (Luke 4:18). This is interpreted in the Gospel according to Luke; for how he entered the synagogue in Capernaum, 'and the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him' (Luke 4:17), so that it might be read, he said: 'and all were marveling at the words of grace proceeding from his mouth' (Luke 4:18). In this way his words are grace-filled as to hold those who hear. He says 'hearing' according to understanding, not according to mere hearing; for all hear the gospel, and 'Greeks and Jews' (Rom 1:16), but they are not [possessing] the grace of the words. Is it necessary to have another person here? 'Grace was poured out on your lips,' that is, the Holy Spirit, or the writer says this.

Sometimes also the Father, witnessing, says; for lips many times we have spoken to signify the word: 'and' for 'unjust lips, keep far from me' (Ps 124:7). 'Because of this, may God your God bless you forever' (Deut 33:29). And this is said also concerning the man; for to be blessed with a cause is not of the word of God. He himself is the blessing, the source of blessing. The 'cause' lies here in the 'because of this,' just as also in: 'because of this God your God has anointed you' (Deut 33:29).

english: Your thigh, powerful one. Therefore we say: the faithful man, the self-controlled one, the imitator of God, girds the unyielding Word of God, which is being wielded above every sword, around his thigh, so that he may cut away superfluous desires. For he who has grasped the honorable marriage and keeps the bed undefiled, has the sword of the Word of God cutting them away.

If 'powerful' here refers to the God-Word or the soul joined to Him, 'thigh' refers to the incarnation, the birth from a woman. Therefore, preserve this sword while your beauty and your loveliness remain. And beauty and loveliness are sinlessness, when spoken of the soul; for it did not know sin. But if spoken of the God-Word, this he says: the beauty and the loveliness of God remain to you, having become man; for you did not change from being the Word and God-Word.

And to each of the rest of the temperate it is said: put on beauty and loveliness from the other virtues, take also temperance, the Word that cuts. But what kind of sword should we take? The Word concerning temperance, the Word in general, the one that cuts. Behold, a wise man is subject to reproof. This one, progressing and beginning, is so. But the perfect one is imperturbable; he is not subject to reproof, he does not deviate from the mouth, that is, the Word, the God. 'Make it known to the righteous, and he will add to receiving' (Psalm 112:9); and 'his righteousness is the first argument'. He entirely possesses what he has argued for himself. But the truly perfect righteous one is not...
the grinding of teeth

source_text: λέοντας ἐπήγαγεν ἐπ' αὐτούς, οὐ δράκοντας, οὐ τοὺς ἄλλους μεγάλους θῆρας, ἀλλὰ σκνῖπα καὶ κυνόμυιαν ἐπὶ βατράχῳ καὶ κάμπῃ. ἐπερ · τὸ "3κατεπόντισεν"3 τί; –ἀλλὰ ἐκεῖ οὐ λέγει· "ἐνπέπαιχα αὐτούς". 14 ῥομφαίαν ἐσπάσαντο οἱ ἁμαρτωλοὶ καὶ ἐνέτειναν τόξον αὐτῶν τοῦ καταβαλεῖν πτωχὸν καὶ πένητα. ἡτοίμασαν ῥομφαίαν, ἵνα πτωχὸν καὶ πένητα καταβάλωσιν. ἀναστρέφεται καὶ εἰς τὴν αὐτῶν ἔρχεται καρδίαν, ὡς τὸ λεγόμενον· "ὁ ὀρύσσων βόθρον τῷ πλησίον ἐνπεσεῖται εἰς αὐτόν". καὶ πάλιν· "καὶ ἡ θήρα, ἣ ἔκρυψαν, συνλαβέτω αὐτούς". καὶ ἐν Ἐκκλησιαστῇ λέγει· "καθαιροῦντα φραγμόν, δήξεται ὄφις". τὸν ἄλλου φραγμὸν καθαιροῦντα ὄφις δήξεται, τὴν ἀσφάλειαν ἄλλου καθαιροῦντα. "καὶ ἡ γλῶσσα αὐτῶν μάχαιρα ὀξεῖα"· ὁ λ̣όγος αὐτῶν οἷα μάχαιρα βλάπτει καὶ τιτρώσκει. ἐν τῷ λέγειν οὖν εἰσίν τινες τιτρώσκοντες μαχαίρᾳ, αἱ δὲ τῶν σοφῶν γλῶσσαι, οἱ λόγοι τῶν σοφῶν, ἰῶνται. αἱ μάχαιραι αὗται φαρμάκου εἰσίν, οὐ τιτρώσκουσιν, οὐ πλήττουσιν, ο̣υ᾿̣ τ̣ρ̣αυματίζουσιν, ἀλλ' ἰῶνται τὰ γενόμενα ὑπ' ἄλλων λόγων τραύματα. τόξον ἐστὶν ἐντεινόμενον τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν τὸ οὕτως ἑτοιμασμένον ὥστε βέλη ἀπ' αὐτοῦ ἀπολύεσθαι. οὗτοι δὲ ἔστωσαν πονηροὶ λογισμοί, λόγοι βλαπτικοί. english: A poor and needy person, even if the heart seems straight, as previously said, like the one being reproved who is wise and the accuser who is righteous of himself; but rather the sword, turned against those who have become blunt, strikes and destroys them; likewise the bow is broken. And it is well to say: 'Let their sword enter into their heart.' This sword, which is harmful, the one of the enemies, is not continuous [text gapped] and in days of famine they shall be satisfied [text gapped] of those feeding the soul, those watering it.

In the prophet, indeed, it is said, where it is written: 'I will bring a famine upon the earth, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord' (Amos 8:11), it is applied: 'Many have fallen in every place, I will cast down silence' (Psalm 142:6). To the fallen, the famine is. To these, however, the silence of the divine word is brought. Thus, 'in days of famine they shall be satisfied.' Because the sinners shall perish.

Twice again we perceive the destruction of the sinners: namely, in the way they are sinners, they perish having experienced the oppressors. The righteous 'are not ashamed in evil time' (2 Timothy 2:15), but the sinners are ashamed. When they are ashamed, knowing how evil they are, and they blush because of sinning, sometimes they despise the sin and become free from it, and thus they perish in such a way that they are no longer sinners.

But the enemies of the Lord, at the same time as they are to be glorified and exalted, having vanished like smoke, they vanished. Sinners are able to be enemies of the Lord. And it is possible also to call sinners those who sin according to ethics, those who transgress the divine commandments, and enemies of the Lord those who think impiously, those outside godliness, those who falsely glorify. These, therefore, are the enemies of the Lord, who at the same time as being to be glorified and exalted immediately vanished like smoke. And behold, always he likens sinners to smoke. And in another psalm it is said: 'As smoke vanishes, so they vanished; as wax melts from before the fire, so the sinners shall perish from before the face of God' (Psalm 68:2).

The word constructs the argument, that the sinners are not of another nature. The smoke is a follower of fire, and the wax of honey. And previously the honey takes origin. Since it does not consist otherwise than in wax, the wax by habit consists. Not because of the wax the honey, but because of the honey the wax, and not because of the smoke the fire, but because of the fire the smoke. The sinners, therefore, according to the smoke, vanish having a following; for sinning itself and enmity toward [the Lord]...

english: Sin is a follower of virtue. The rational animal has become capable of virtue. Yet this capability is not an essence of any kind. Humans are not good by essence; for they were created so that they might become good through participation in the truly good. But the capacity for evil follows the capacity for virtue. Just as the bad always follows the good, bad art follows art, and mishearing follows hearing. Sin, therefore, is a follower of virtue; the sinning animal would not exist if it were not capable of virtue.

Similarly, wax is a follower. For this [substance] does not turn into non-existence, but changes into something better. And sinners become smoke because of this very evil; for lawlessness is in a certain way like a harmful eye or smoke to the eyes. You see that lawlessness becomes to those using it like smoke to the eyes. Smoke does not need great force to be overturned, for it is quickly overturned. Therefore, sinners are 'as wax melts from the presence of fire,' and 'as smoke vanishes, so let them vanish.' Smoke is, as I have said, a follower of fire; for it exists because fire exists or comes to be.

Thus the enemies of the Lord, even if they blaze brightly and are praised as capable or promising, are extinguished like smoke at the very moment they are exalted. It is ours to see their vanishing; for even if they remain for a time, being glorified and praised and thinking great things, those able to see that which they think great find them instantly vanishing. 'The borrower does not repay' (Psalm 36:28).

What God gives for the benefit of humans and the soul, those receiving do not take as a debt; for no one receives anything in this age as a debt, but giving as a gift, the good man gives a loan so that, having worked with it, he may gain and give interest. I take the word concerning righteousness. If I give back and also provide interest, I offer the works of righteousness to God. But if, having received the word concerning righteousness, I do nothing according to righteousness, having borrowed from God, I have not repaid; for God gives so that we may act, and God provides so that we may turn words into deeds. His divine silver is lent, concerning which it is said, 'silver refined is a test for the earth' (Psalm 66:3). The borrower therefore pays back interest and also that which he received. But the righteous man shows mercy and gives.
